characteristics.$text: When allocating Melee Attacks, each attack must choose a target. All attacks of the given Agility Step must be allocated before determining the number of hits. Viable targets are: • Rank-and-File models in any unit whose Unit Boundary (see Definitions and Terminology chapter) the attacker is in contact with. • Any Attachable Model that the attacker is in contact with. If a model is making Supporting Attacks, it can allocate its attacks as if it was located in the Front Rank of the unit, in the same file.

characteristics.$text: Models with Ambush may be deployed using Special Deployment rules. All models that will be deployed using the Ambush rule must be declared during step 7 of the Pre-Game Sequence (after Determining Deployment Zones), starting with the player that picked the Deployment Zone first. Deploy your warband as usual, but without the Ambushing models. Starting with your Player Turn 2, immediately after step 3 of each friendly Movement Phase Sequence (after moving models with Random Movement), roll a dice for each of your Ambushing models. After rolling for all Ambushers, models that rolled 3+ enter the Battlefield from any Table Edge. Place the arriving models in contact with the Table Edge. Ambushers are subject to the following rules and restrictions: • Ambushing models cannot make March Move during the Movement Phase in which they arrive. • Ambushing models count as having moved during the Player Turn they arrive on the Battlefield for the purpose of shooting. • Until an Ambushing model arrives at the battlefield, it counts as Delayed for all intents and purposes (including Rout Checks). • If an Ambushing model has not entered the Battlefield before the end of the game (e.g. due to failing all its 3+ rolls), the model counts as having been Removed.

characteristics.$text: Before making a Shooting Attack with Area Attack, determine the attack’s Target Facing using the same rules as for Cover. • If the attack hits in the Front or Rear: select up to Y different ranks of the target. • If the attack hits in the Flank: select up to Y different files of the target. For each rank or file chosen this way, the unit takes X hits, up to a maximum equal to the number of models in that rank or file. An Area Attack can not cause more hits than the total models in the unit, and no single model can suffer more than one hit from each Area Attack. Remember that attacks multiplied into several hits are allocated after establishing how many hits are scored (i.e. after the attack has hit). Figure figure/areaattack illustrates different variations of Area Attack. Examples of Area Attacks. Units A to D are hit by an Area Attack (33) that has their Front as its Target Facing. A: There are 3 ranks with more than 3 models. Number of hits: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. B: The first rank has more than 3 models, but the second rank only has 2 models. There is no third rank. Number of hits: 3 + 2 = 5. C: Since there is only a single model, there will always only be a single rank with a single model. Number of hits: 1. D: The first and second rank have 3 models. There is no third rank. Number of hits: 3 + 3 = 6. Units E and F are hit by an Area Attack (14). E: The attack has the Front of the unit as its Target Facing. The first and second rank have more than 1 model. There is no third or fourth rank. Number of hits: 1 + 1 = 2. F: The attack has the Flank of the unit as its Target Facing. There are more than 4 files with 1 or more models. Number of hits: 1 + 1 +1 +1 = 4.

characteristics.$text: These upgrades apply to pieces of armour carried by a model, and can in general be taken by any model. That model is then considered as wearing an Enchanted Armour. If an Armour Enchantment is restricted to models with a minimum Armour value, for this purpose only consider the model’s part unmodified base Armour value (excluding mounts), the number written on its profile in the Army Book. The following rules apply to all Armour Enchantments, unless specifically mentioned otherwise: • Characteristics modifiers, Model Rules, and all other rules associated with Armour Enchantments are generally only applied to the model part wearing the Enchanted Armour, and do not affect other model parts such as mounts. This includes modifiers to Global and Defensive Characteristics. However, note that certain Model Rules, particularly Model Rules that are neither an Attack Attribute nor a weapon, are always applied to the combined model (and not only to individual model parts). For example the Basalt Infusion provides +1 Arm and Aegis. +1 Arm is a Characteristic modifier, and is thus only applied to the Character wearing the Enchanted Armour. If this Character rides a mount that has its own Armour value, the Armour modifier from Basalt Infusion has no effect on the combined model. However, Aegis is a Global Model Rule, which means it is not applied to an individual model part, but to the whole combined model.

characteristics.$text: Attachable Models are models that have the flexibility to join other units as well as to operate by themselves. The most common type of Attachable Models are Characters. characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Attack Attributes is a subcategory of Model Rules. While most Model Rules apply to the entire model (including all model parts on the same base), Attack Attributes are an exception, and only affect individual model parts, or even individual attacks. Attack Attributes only affect Melee Attacks, unless otherwise stated. There is one main exception to this: an Attack Attribute given specifically to a weapon, a spell or attack will affects it regardless of whether it would normally only be applicable to Melee Attacks. Attack Attributes are therefore written under the Offensive Characteristics part of a model entry, only affecting the specific model part they are listed under. However, if an Attack Attribute is given to a unit (e.g. as a result of a spell), it applies to every model part in that unit; if given to a model, it applies to all parts of that model. An Attack Attribute can also be given to a weapon, a spell, or an attack. Such Attack Attributes only affect attacks made with those specific sources. They will not affect other attacks made by the same model part (unless given specifically to another weapon, spell or attack by that model part).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When conducting an attack, follow this sequence: 1 & The attacker allocates its attacks to a target. 2 & Determine the number of hits. If at least one hit is caused, proceed. 3 & The attacker rolls to wound. If successful, proceed. 4 & The defender rolls Armour Saves. If failed, proceed. 5 & The defender rolls Special Saves. If failed, proceed. 6 & The defender suffers unsaved wounds, loses Health Points and removes casualties. 7 & The defender takes Panic Tests if necessary. Complete each step for all simultaneous attacks, such as all Shooting Attacks from a single unit or all Melee Attacks at a specific Agility Step, before proceeding to the next step.

This does not let a Caster change the Path of Magic initially chosen during Spell Selection as part of Pre-game Planning, if the Caster did not select a Path of Magic, then this is not relevant.

characteristics.$text: The winner of the game is determined by the number of Battle Points they score. Players always share a total of 20 Battle Points, making a 10-10 a draw and a 20-0 a decisive victory. Battle Points can be scored in three ways: • Victory Points: the primary way to score Battle Points is by defeating enemy units, which gives you Victory Points (VP) (see below for details on how many VP units give). • Winning the Primary Objective: each player competes for the same Primary Objective, selected at the start of the game. The player who wins the Primary Objective scores 3 Battle Points, while the other player loses 3 Battle Points. • Completing Secondary Objectives: each player usually has one Secondary Objective, selected at the start of the game. For each Secondary Objective a player completes, they score 1 Battle Point, while their opponent loses 1 Battle Point (which means that if each player completes an equal number of Secondary Objectives, the score does not change). If no outside source tells you how to use Secondary Objectives (e.g. tournament organiser, campaign rules, etc.), players should establish how much they want to focus on Secondary Objectives before the game. Consider the following guidelines: • In standard competitive games, Secondary Objectives are typically worth +1/-1 BP, as detailed in the table below. • For games focused on learning the core rules, it is recommended to ignore Secondary Objectives entirely. • Those seeking a more immersive, story-driven experience may opt to assign a higher value to Secondary Objectives, such as +5/-5 BP. Players are encouraged to assign a value for Secondary Objectives corresponding to their desired level of competitive challenge and narrative engagement. Scoring Victory Points At the end of the game, each player earns Victory Points (VP) using the rules below. • Destroyed Units: you gain a number of VP equal to the full Points Cost (as stated on the Army List) of each enemy unit that has been removed as a casualty. • Shaken Units: you gain a number of VP equal to half the Points Cost (as stated on the Army List, and rounding fractions up) of each enemy Unit that is Shaken at the end of the game. • Decimated Units: you gain a number of VP equal to half the Points Cost (as stated on the Army List, and rounding fractions up) of each enemy unit that is Decimated at the end of the game (so that each enemy unit that is both Shaken and Decimated at the end of the game gives you its full Points Cost in VP). • When calculating VP, Attachable Models are considered separately from the units they are joined to at the end of the game. After summing all Victory Points for both players, calculate the difference between the amount gained by each player. Compare that difference to the Army Size, and check the table below to convert Victory Points to Battle Points. This means that player A receives 14 Battle Points, and player B, 6 Battle Points. • Player A won the Primary Objective, which modifies the result into 17-3. • Both players completed their Secondary Objective: the result is thus not further modified. *If it was decided to increase the value of Secondary Objectives before the game, modify these values accordingly.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Before battle can be joined, you must establish the nature of the battlefield, the armies that will fight upon it, and their reason for being there. This is a natural part of setting up the game, but it can also represent a commander reviewing their troops and scouting the land in preparation for an important battle. When preparing to play a game of The 9th Age: Skirmish Campaigns, players follow a series of steps: & • Pre-game Planning usually done before players arrive to the gaming table • Decide Army Size, which determines the scale of the game. This can be done by the players agreeing on an Army Size, or an outside source such as campaign rules or a tournament organiser dictating this. • Build an Army. Each player creates an Army List from one of the Army Books. • Community Tools details of gaming aids, in particular the digital army builder New Recruit. • Initial Preparations these are sometimes done before arrival (typical in a tournament setting). • Share Army Lists with your opponent, revealing the units and options you will be using during the game. • Build the Battlefield by setting up terrain and scenery to create an engaging and challenging environment for the battle. • Determine Deployment Type – this defines where on the Battlefield the armies can start. • Determine and Setup Victory Conditions which defines the primary goal for the battle. • Battle Setup (these actions are done at the gaming table by both players together) • Roll-off for Attacker and Defender: the players each roll a dice, the winner decides which player is going to be the Defender; the other will be the Attacker. • Determine Secondary Objectives if Secondary Objectives are used, determine these now. • Defenders Pre-game Selections the Defender selects a Deployment Zone, and performs all their Pre-game Selections. Common selections include targets for Secondary Objectives and Spell Swaps. • Attackers Pre-game Selections the Attacker performs all their Pre-game Selections. Common choices include targets for Secondary Objectives and Spell Swaps. • Deploy units: both players place their units, starting with the Attacker, entirely within their Deployment Zones. • Vanguard Units the Defender gives Vanguard (3") to one of their units and performs the first Vanguard Move with this unit. The Season Pack is an annually updated supplement that can provide support in building a battlefield and add several variations on Deployment Types, Primary Objectives and Secondary Objectives. If you are looking for a fast and simple game, or if this is one of your first games, we recommend you use the rules below and leave the Season Pack until next time.

characteristics.$text: The Battlefield Edge represents the boundaries of the game. A unit is allowed to temporarily and partially move off the Battlefield during a Movement Manoeuvre or Charge Move, with the following restrictions: • The unit’s Front Facing must remain entirely on the board at all times, except during Align Moves where it just needs to end entirely on the board. • The unit must finish any movement with its Unit Boundary entirely on the Battlefield.

characteristics.$text: To prevent abusive situations where a unit cannot Charge a nearby unit due to convoluted positioning of enemy units, the following rules are applied. Blocked Path can only be applied against enemy units that fullfil all of the following criteria: • The enemy unit is directly in front of your unit. This means that the first obstacle (other unit or Impassable Terrain) that a straight Forward Move of your unit would hit is an enemy unit. • Your unit would be unable to perform a Charge Move to get into contact with the Target Facing of the enemy unit. • The Charge is not made impossible due to friendly units Engaged with the Target Facing of the enemy unit. (i.e. Blocked Path is not applicable if the Charge is made impossible due to your own units being Engaged with the Target Facing) In this situation, your unit may Declare a Charge towards the enemy unit, and if the enemy does not Flee, use the Facing that is adjacent to the Target Facing and closest to your Charging Unit (and perform a Charge Move as normal towards this new Target Facing).

characteristics.$text: Casting and dispelling Bound Spells follow the normal procedure for casting a Learned Spell, with the following exceptions: • Bound Spells have their own Casting Values, defined in the brackets following Bound Spell. • When trying to cast a Bound Spell, one Magic Dice is a D6, the rest are D3. For example, if casting a Bound Spell using 3 Magic Dice, roll 1D6 and 2D3. • A rolled D3 can never Fizzle. • Bound Spells can never Miscast. When casting a Bound Spell version of a spell for which a casting attempt was already made in the same Magic Phase, the Casting Roll is decreased only by -1 (instead of by -3). Note: when attempting to cast a Learned Spell version of a Bound Spell for which a casting attempt was already made in the same Magic Phase, the Casting Roll is still decreased by -3, as usual. This penalty is ignored if the spell is Replicable. Bound Spells are designed to offer low-resource and low-risk casting opportunities to the players. They typically require fewer dice for casting and never cause Miscasts. However, they are also easier to dispel. As a result, Bound Spells are the perfect tool when the opponent is out of Magic Dice for dispelling. When casting Bound Spells, it is important to clearly differentiate the D6s and the D3s. Announce to the opponent how you roll your dice, and either roll them separately, use differently coloured dice, or use dedicated D3-only dice.

characteristics.$text: As the player, it is your duty to command your army on the battlefield, but first you will have to pick one of the different factions available to you. Each Army Book contains a description of the different units that are available to its faction, as well as their Characteristics and special rules. To build your army, you must write an Army List, which details the selection of units, spells and options you want to use, along with their Points Cost. Every unit, weapon, upgrade, and Magic Item has a specific Points Cost, which is used to balance the game and ensure fair play between the players. Planning, strategy, knowing terrain, learning about the ponent – very useful for a heist! What? You were asking about battles? Oh yes, Klepa knows them too. We goblins are Warborn after all – that’s the name us and orc pals call ourselves together. Klepa has seen all the great battles, seen loads of action! Normally from quite far away – so you know I had a good view. Main thing I’ve learned is you’ve got to get there early if you want the best spot for hiding and picking over the loot at the end. You want some loot? Genuine, authentikarated battle gear, picked from the choiciest corpses! Just step quietly over to Appendicitis Numero Two and we’ll have a little chat about the low low prices. Army Books The rules for playing the various factions are detailed in the Army Books and supplement Army Books (remember that using a supplement requires the agreement of your opponent or event organiser). Unit Entries Each entry in an Army Book belongs to a specific Army Category, represented by one or several specific icons in the Army Book. Each Army Category has its own Points Cost limit, as defined in the Army Book, determining how many Army Points a player can allocate to that particular category. This allows players to create a balanced and strategic army composition for their games. An army can typically spend up to 40% of its Army Points on characters. All entries in this Category follow the rules for both Characters and Attachable Models. Characters are the leaders and exceptional individuals in the army, wielding various skills such as brute force, tactical acumen, spellcasting ability, or engineering knowledge. They play a crucial role in influencing the outcome of battles, and one of them usually serves as the army’s General, responsible for leading and inspiring your forces. An army must spend a minimum number of Army Points on this category generally 25%. Core units represent the most readily available warriors in the faction, serving as essential rank-and-file troops under the command of the Characters. They are always present in some combination as part of your fighting force. This Army Category has no maximum limit. An army can spend any amount of Army Points on units in this Category. The Special Army Category represents less common and more unique forces that are found in some but not all of your faction’s armies. While they might make up the largest portion of your host, the availability of each unit is still limited. They usually fill a range of useful and impactful roles. An Army-Specific Category always has a maximum percentage of Army Points that can be spent on it; the limit is defined in the individual Army Books. Army-Specific Categories introduce additional options and limitations in army building, reflecting the nature of the faction. Army-Specific Categories can include thematic groupings of units, limitations based on specific functions, and the faction’s most rare and powerful forces. Units belonging to more than one Army Category Some units can be included in more than one Army Category, which is represented by more than one icon in their entry. In these cases, simply count the unit’s Points Cost towards the limits of all its Army Categories, but only once towards the army’s Points Cost. Adding Army Categories to a Unit Choosing certain options can make a unit count towards another Army Category in addition to its original Army Category. For example, giving a unit Shooting Weapons might make it also count towards the Ranged Support Army Category. This is marked by a small icon of the additional Army Category, displayed underneath the original Army Category icon(s), together with the conditions for counting towards this additional Army Category. Splitting Point Cost between Army Categories In a few cases, a unit’s Points Cost can be split between different Army Categories, where the Points Cost for some particular option is additionally counted towards a different Army Category than the unit. This is marked in the unit entry by a split icon, with the two halves representing the two Army Categories the unit counts towards. For example, a 250 pts Elf Character, counted towards the Characters Army Category, decides to ride a 500 pts Dragon, which is an option marked to count additionally towards Beasts and Monsters. In this case, the player must count the entire unit’s Points Cost (250 + 500 = 750 pts) towards Characters, and the Dragon’s Points Cost (500 pts) towards Beasts and Monsters. Of course, only 750 pts are added towards the army’s total limit. Rarity – Restrictions for Units and Items All units and some options in the army have a limit on the number of times, that they can be included in the army. • • Max. X items per army: some items have a number of Max. X allowed per army. Eg. Max. 20 bows, Max. 4 models. This means you can only include a maximum of X instances of each of these items in your army. • Regular: these Unit Entries are limited to a maximum of 1 per 500 Army Points (rounding fractions up). For example, at 4000 Army Points, Regular Unit Entries are restricted to Max. 8/army). Generally units taken from the Core Army Category are Regular. • Ordinary: these Unit Entries are limited to a maximum of 1 per 750 Army Points (rounding fractions up). For example, at 4000 Army Points, Ordinary Unit Entries are restricted to ‘Max. 6/army’). • Common: these items are limited to a maximum of 1 per 1000 Army Points (rounding fractions up). For example, at 4000 Army Points, Common items are restricted to Max. 4/army). This is the default limit for all Unit Entries. • Uncommon: these items are limited to a maximum of 1 per 1500 Army Points (rounding fractions up). For example, at 4000 Army Points, Uncommon items are restricted to Max. 3/army). This is the least restrictive limit generally used on magical items and unusual mounts. • Rare: these items are limited to a maximum of 1 per 2500 Army Points (rounding fractions up). For example, at 4000 Army Points, Rare items are restricted to Max. 2/army). Monsters, elite knights and powerful war machines usually follow this limit. • Extraordinary: these items are limited to a maximum of 1 per 5000 Army Points (rounding fractions up). For example, at 4000 Army Points, Extraordinary items are restricted to Max. 1/army). Army defining entries generally follow this limit, such as magical altars, faction unique upgrades and the most ancient of dragons. • Legendary: these items can only ever be taken once per army. Most magic items, the Battle Standard Bearer and the General follow this limit. • Max. X combined items per army: some combinations of items may be restricted in combination. In these cases this will be detailed in the Army Organisation part of the Army Book. This is usually units that can have a Character mounted on them, or it is a unit with a shooting and melee variant. • Max. X items per unit: some items have a maximum limitation allowed per unit. This means you can choose to include up to X instances of these items (mounts, upgrades, etc.) for each unit. If a single model part has multiple items that count against the same limit, it only counts once against this limit using the highest ratio. 0.75orcKing.png

characteristics.$text: While the game is playable on a wide variety of Battlefields of all dimensions, we recommend that the following sizes are adhered to. This provides a good balance between having enough room to manoeuvre your troops, and not having so much room that hardly any engagements happen. • Battlefield Size: the game is played on a rectangular Battlefield, with two main dimensions: • Short Battlefield Edge: the main direction along which the two opposing armies face each other. We recommend this to be 48" (roughly 120 cm), regardless of Army Size. • Long Battlefield Edge: in most Deployment Types, the long Battlefield Edge is the side along which the units of each army is lined up. The bigger the armies are, the longer the Battlefield Edge you need to fit all the units. See the table beside for recommendations. • Terrain placement: the terrain on the Battlefield is essential for adding depth and strategic elements to the game. It can represent various features, from simple objects to more significant landmarks. Players have the flexibility to determine the size, type, and number of Terrain Features, as well as their placement. Prebuilt Battlefield maps are available in the Season Pack.
