characteristics.$text: Determine which side won this Round of Combat. This is done by adding the Casualty-based Combat Score bonuses to the previously calculated Static Combat Score bonuses The side with the higher Combat Score wins, while the side with the lower Combat Score loses. In case of a tie, both sides are considered winners. A unit that is no longer in contact with any enemy units always counts as having won the Round of Combat.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The goal of a Round of Combat is to annihilate or rout the enemy, the latter is done through winning the Round of Combat, by having your units accumulate a higher total Combat Score than the opponent’s units. The Combat Score is calculated at two different steps: • First in step 2 of the Round of Combat Sequence (Combat Set-Up), where Static Combat Score bonuses are added up and marked down. • After all attacks have been made, at step 4 of the Round of Combat Sequence (Determine the Winner), Casualty-based Combat Score bonuses are added to calculate the final Combat Score. The Static Combat Score bonuses are: • Charge: +1 Each side with one or more Charging units adds +1 to their Combat Score. • Fighting on the Flanks or the Rear: +2 / each Flank or Rear If a side has units fighting the enemy in their Flank or Rear, it adds +2 to its Combat Score for each different Flank or Rear Facing of each enemy unit it has units Engaged on. • Rank Bonus: +1 / Proper Rank (up to +4) Each side adds to its Combat Score the number of Proper Ranks of its unit that has the most Proper Ranks, up to a maximum of +4. Note that the Rank Bonus of a unit can be reduced if it is Surrounded. See Models and Units in the Definitions and Terminology chapter for the definition of Proper Rank. • Standard Bearer: +1 / Standard Bearer Each side adds +1 to its Combat Score for each units with a Standard Bearer Engaged in the Combat. • Other Modifiers Additional modifiers can be added to each side’s Combat Score (such as +1 if the Battle Standard Bearer is Engaged in the Combat). Combats can be messy and time-consuming to resolve. To simplify the process, we recommend placing special dice or markers next to the units to track the Static Combat Score.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A unit containing Captain gains the following additional rules: • If the unit has a Standard Bearer, it is considered to be within range of its Battle Standard Bearer’s* Beacon of Courage rule. • If the unit has a Musician, it is considered to be within range of its Leader’s* Commanding Presence rule. A unit can only contain a single Attachable Model with Captain. *Provided such a model is on the Battlefield at all.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each of the Active Player’s models with one or more spells can attempt to cast each spell up to once per Magic Phase. (Remember that Shaken models cannot cast spells.) The sequence for casting a spell is as follows: Well no, I’m not a magician myself; I am a scholar, and one of the finest minds in Avras, I’ll have you know! And I have read all there is to know about magic, including the drivel that Heisermann calls his magnum opus. Any true wizard will tell you that magic comes at a cost; too much of the stuff is lethal. It’s a mutagenic poison, after all. A withering, corrupting substance. And those with the proper training can feel the limits of what their body can tolerate instinctively – they cannot use more than is good for them any more than you could stop breathing. Casting Roll – Active Player 1 & Caster and target: declare which model is casting what spell, and choose a target (or targets) for the spell (for details, see Spell Types in the Arcane Compendium). 2 & Spend Magic Dice to cast: declare how many Magic Dice are spent on the Casting Roll (at least 2 Magic Dice must be used, and at most 5 Magic Dice can be used). 3 & Roll Dice: roll the Magic Dice used for the Casting Roll, and add the results together. If the total is equal to or above the spell’s Casting Value, the casting is successful. Otherwise, the Casting Roll failed: go directly to step 7. • Fizzle: if one or more ‘1’ was rolled, and the Casting Roll was not successful, each dice that rolled a ‘1’ is added back to the Magic Dice pool. • Miscast: if three or more Magic Dice – or two Magic Dice if using only two dice – used for the Casting Roll gave an identical result, and the Casting Roll is successful, and the spell is not dispelled, a Miscast occurs. Consult the Miscast Table for further instructions. Dispelling Roll - Reactive Player 4 & Spend Magic Dice to dispel: the Reactive Player may try to dispel the spell. If not, go directly to step 6. If the Reactive Player chooses to try to dispel, they declare how many Magic Dice are spent on the Dispelling Roll. Note: there are no limits to how many or how few Magic Dice the Reactive Player may use for this. 5 & Dispelling Roll: roll the Magic Dice used for the Dispelling Roll, and add the results together. If the total is equal to or above the Casting Roll, the dispel is successful: proceed to step 7. Otherwise, the Dispelling Roll failed: proceed to step 6. • Fizzle: if one or more ‘1’ was rolled, and the Dispelling Roll was not successful, each dice that rolled a ‘1’ is added back to the Magic Dice pool. Resolving the spell effect 6 & Apply Spell effects: if the Casting Roll was successful, and the spell was not dispelled, it is successfully cast. Apply the spell effects. Spell effects are never affected by any effects affecting the Caster, including Magic Items, Model Rules, other spell effects, or similar abilities, unless specifically stated otherwise. Removing the Caster of a spell as a casualty does not affect the spells duration. 7 & Next casting attempt: afterward, the Active Player may attempt to cast other spells, provided they have enough Magic Dice left.

sharedProfiles.name: Casting Multiple Instances of the Same Spell

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each Caster may only try to cast each of its Learned Spells once per Magic Phase, and may try to cast a Bound Spell once for every instance of that spell it has. If multiple Casters know the same spell, all of them may try to cast their instance(s) of the spell. When attempting to cast a Learned Spell when a casting attempt (successful or not) has already been made for another instance of the same spell (either Bound or Learned), then the Casting Roll is reduced by -3, and by another -3 for each additional attempt in the same phase. For example, if two casting attempts have already been made for different instances of the same spell, any third attempt to cast it will suffer a -6 penalty to its Casting Roll. If the additional casting attempt is made for a Bound Spell version of the same spell, the Casting Roll is only reduced by -1, instead of by -3, for each previous casting attempt for a version of the same spell. Remember that Replicable Spells ignore this penalty to multiple casting attempts.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each unsaved wound reduces the Health Pool by 1 Health Point. • If the models in the attacked Heath Pool have 1 Health Point each, remove one model for each Health Point lost. • If the models have more than 1 Health Point each, remove entire models whenever possible. Keep track of any lost Health Points that are not enough to remove a whole model, as they will be taken into account for future attacks. For example, a unit of 10 Trolls (3 Health Points each) loses 7 Health Points: remove two whole models (6 Health Points), leaving 1 lost Health Point, which is kept track of. Later, this unit loses 2 Health Points, which is enough to remove a single Troll, since 1 Health Point was lost from the previous attack. When there are more Health Point losses than there are Health Points in a Health Pool, the excess losses are ignored. In situations where simultaneous attacks from different model parts, models, or units cause excess Health Point losses, the owner of the attacking models decides which attacks caused the excess losses (if relevant). When enough Health Points are lost to remove models, do so from as far back in the unit as possible. In certain situations, additional nuances for casualty removal are needed. In such cases, follow the procedure below: • Remove models from as far back in the unit as possible. • Remove models one by one, in any chosen order. • When casualties are removed from the first rank, remove models equally from both sides of the unit, one by one. This applies only to each batch of simultaneous losses. • If a model of a different Health Pool is in a position that would normally be removed as a casualty, remove the next eligible model of the attacked Health Pool and redistribute the models in the unit into a viable formation (see Maintaining a Viable Formation in the Definitions and Terminology chapter). If the removal of casualties would lead to a non-viable unit formation, such as gaps being created in ranks other than the last, follow the procedure described in the Reference Handbook under Maintaining a Viable Formation, in the Definitions and Terminology chapter.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When an Engaged unit suffers Casualties outside the Melee Phase, apply the following rules: • When casualties would be removed from the first rank, instead of removing models equally from both sides of the unit, remove models from the side that avoids making Engaged units lose Contact with each other. • If unavoidable, prioritize creating gaps where as many units as possible can be nudged back into contact. • If gaps are created between units, follow the rules under Nudge Units to Maintain Contact (see the Melee Phase chapter).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Once all Agility Steps have been resolved, i.e. all models have had a chance to attack, the Casualty-based Combat Score is calculated. The Casualty-based Combat Score bonuses are: • Health Point losses caused on enemy units: +1 / Health Point Add up the number of Health Points lost by your opponent’s units during the Round of Combat. • Wiped enemy unit: +1 / unit Add +1 for each enemy unit where all the unit’s models were removed as casualties (in addition to the Health Points losses incurred by those units before being wiped out). This includes Shaken units that were removed at the start of the Round of Combat; however, Shaken units only contribute with +1 for being wiped, no Health Point losses are taken into account.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A model with Channel may add X Magic Dice during the Siphon the Veil step of its Magic Phase. Note: Shaken models may not use this rule.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When a Character selects a mount from the options available to it, the following rules apply to the combined model of a rider and its mount: • Height and Base: use the Mount’s Height and base. • Offence Characteristics: the rider and the mount each use their own Offensive Characteristics, Weapons and Attack Attributes. • Defence and Global Characteristics: the combined model has a single set of Global and Defensive Characteristics and Model Rules. • Generally, the values from the mount’s profile are used. Modifiers to the rider’s Characteristics have no impact on the Global and Defence Characteristics of the mount, unless specifically mentioned otherwise, or in of the following: • If a value in the mount’s profile is indicated as C, the corresponding value from the Character’s profile is used instead, including any modifiers to it. • If a value is written as C+X, increase the Character’s value by X, and use that value as the whole model’s. • If a value is written as C–X, decrease the Character’s value by X, and use that value as the whole model´s. • For example, a Character with Arm 2 is using a Shield (+1 Arm) while mounted on a Dragon with Arm 4: the combined model’s Armour value is still only 4 (the Dragon’s). If the same Character is instead mounted on a Warhorse with Arm C+2, the model’s Armour value is 5 (2+1+2). • Model Rules: Model Rules also follow the principles described above, with the following specifications: • Attack Attributes and Weapons are applied only to the specific model part that has those rules. • Other Model Rules are applied to the combined model as a whole. • For example, a Character with Distracting, Lethal Strike is mounted on a Warhorse. The horse cannot benefit from Lethal Strike: since it is an Attack Attribute, it applies only to attacks from a single model part, the Character itself. However, Distracting is neither an Attack Attribute nor a Weapon, and is therefore applied to the entire combined model.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each unit entry contains three Characteristic Profiles: Global, Defensive, and Offensive. A higher value of a given Characteristic indicates that a model is more accomplished in that Characteristic. These values are used for various game mechanics like moving units and attacking with models. Some model parts may not have specific values for certain Characteristics, such as the chassis of a chariot without Offensive Skill. These Characteristics are considered to be 0, and cannot be modified in any way.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Character is a significant and unique individual in the army, often possessing special abilities, skills, or powers that set them apart from regular troops. Characters are a special type of models that are recruited from the Characters Army Category of an Army Book. Unless stated otherwise, Characters follow the rules for Attachable Models, which means they can join other units.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Charge Move is divided into two sub-moves: first a Snaking Forward Move to get into contact with the target unit, then an Align Move. Start with establishing in what Arc of the target unit, that the centre of the Charging Unit’s Front Facing is located in (see figure above). The Facing that corresponds to this Arc is the Target Facing. See Definitions and Terminology chapter for definitions of Arcs and Facings. A Charge Move is performed using a single Snaking Forward Move (see Movement Phase chapter for details), with an unlimited distance. During this move, the Charging Unit must move into contact with its intended target - The Charging Unit’s Front Facing against the Target Facing. Charge Moves are allowed to end the move within 1" of Impassable Terrain or other units, but are not allowed to move into contact with any enemy unit, other than the target of the Charge. Once the Charging Unit touches its Target Facing, it performs an Align Move. This is done by picking up the Charging Unit and placing it back on the Battlefield aligned with the target unit, in a way that keeps the initial point of contact on the charged unit still in contact, while maximising the number of models in contact. See the Reference Handbook for details on how to prioritise the Initial Align Move in complex situations. Apply the following rules when performing Align Moves. The entire Charge Move must be made in such a way that the Charging Unit can satisfy the following conditions as best as possible, in decreasing order of priority: • The initial point of contact* on the target unit, before the Align Move, must remain in contact* after the Align Move. Note that the Charging model that initially made contact is not required to remain in contact*. • If there is no single initial point of contact*, e.g. because the initial contact* is made along a line, the Charging Unit decides where the initial point of contact* is, among the possible points of initial contact*. This choice must be made such that the conditions below are satisfied as best as possible. • The Charging Unit is fully aligned with its Front Facing flush against the Target Facing. • If this is not possible, apply the rules for Unaligned Charges (see below). • The number of models in the target unit that are in contact* with enemy units must be maximised. This includes Fighting Over Gaps. • The number of models in the Charging Unit that are in contact* with enemy units must be maximised. This includes Fighting Over Gaps. If it is unavoidable to break one or more of the above conditions, prioritise maintaining the higher priority conditions, even if it means breaking a greater number of conditions in total. As long as all the above conditions are satisfied to the best extent possible, the Charging Unit is free to choose how it performs the Align Move. ReferenceManualColorExample of a Charge Move. From left to right.1. Declare Charge: Unit A Declares a Charge towards unit B. 2. Initial Forward: Unit A moves straight forward. 3. Wheel: The unit is rotated forward around its front right corner. 4. Concluding Forward: Unit A moves forward again, until it contacts unit B. 5. Align: Unit A is picked up and put back down in contact and fully aligned with unit B. Now me and Fleabag, when we’re working a mark, our most reliable method is the old one-two. It’s a classic for a reason. Go straight in and try to pinch the goods on your lonesome, you’re asking for a pointed intryductshin to a boot or five. But if the hound creeps up one way, and Klepa sidles over from behind, I can often have a leeesurely peroosal of pockets and purses before they know a thing. Teamwork makes the dream work – or as we Warborn say, broodwork makes the mood work!

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: After all Charges and Charge Reactions have been declared and resolved, Charging Units will attempt to move into Combat. Each unit that Declared a Charge in this Phase now rolls its Charge Range and, if successful, performs a Charge Move. Roll and move units one by one.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: In the Charge Phase, your forces will take the initiative, breaking from their ordered manoeuvres to run headlong across the field, with the single purpose of meeting the enemy in Combat. But such Charges are not so simple as they seem; eager troops can hesitate and stumble as the reality of battle approaches, or they might find their target is too far away, allowing the opponent to draw them out of position or rake them with fire before they can reach their ranks.The Charge Phase is an opportunity for the Active Player to move their units into Combat with enemy units by Declaring Charges. It is the primary method of engaging in Close Combat. Never wear red to a minotaur party – that’s one of the classic blunders! The Charge Phase is divided into the following steps: 1 & Start of the Charge Phase (and Player Turn) 2 & Declare Charges • The Active Player chooses one of their units, and Declares a Charge towards an enemy unit. • The Reactive Player declares and resolves the target’s Charge Reaction. • Repeat steps (a) and (b) with your units, one at a time, until all of your units that can and wish to Declare a Charge have done so. 3 & Moves Charges • The Active Player chooses a unit that has Declared a Charge, and rolls its Charge Range roll. If multiple units are charging the same target, make a separate Charge Range roll for every unit Charging the same target. • Perform the Charge Move or Failed Charge Move with the unit(s) you just rolled Charge Range for. • Repeat step 3 for all units that have Declared a Charge this Phase. 4 & End of the Charge Phase.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Roll D6+4 and add the unit’s Charge Speed (see Characteristic Profiles in the Definitions and Terminology chapter). • If the Charge Range is equal to or greater than the distance between the Charging Unit and its intended target (in inches), and if there is enough space to complete the Charge Move (including the Initial Align Move), then the Charge is successful and the Charging Unit performs a Charge Move. • Otherwise, the Charge is failed: the Charging Unit performs a Failed Charge Move. Front or Flank?a) The centre of Charging Unit B’s Front Facing is located in enemy unit A’s Front Arc. b) The Charging Unit must contact the charged unit’s Front Facing. Some players prefer to know their odds when Declaring Charges. Below are the probabilities for the most common cases. Needed score to & 5" & 6" & 7" & 8" & 9" & 10" D6+4 & 100% & 83% & 67% & 50% & 33% & 17% Maximised*D6+4 & 100% & 97% & 89% & 75% & 56% & 31% * Maximised rolls are explained in the Definitions and Terminology chapter.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When a unit has a Charge declared against it, it must immediately perform a Charge Reaction. The owner of the charged unit declares which Charge Reaction it chooses and resolve the effects immediately. There are two Charge Reactions: • Hold! This is the default Charge Reaction. Choosing the Hold! Charge Reaction means the unit stands its ground and takes no further action. • Flee! A unit can select this Charge Reaction only once per Phase, and only if not already Engaged in Combat. The unit is pivoted to face directly away from the Centre of the Charging Unit; it then performs a Flee Move (see the Psychology chapter). • If this Flee Move brings the fleeing unit into contact with a unit that has Declared a Charge against it this Phase, the fleeing unit is immediately removed as a casualty. • Remember that Flee Moves due to the Flee! Charge Reaction, do not cause Panic Tests in friendly units that the Fleeing unit moves through since they are voluntary. This does not apply if forced to Flee! due to being charged by a unit containing Terror.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: If a charged unit has chosen the Flee! Charge Reaction, after its Flee Move has been completed, the unit(s) that Declared a Charge towards it may attempt to Redirect their Charge. To do so, each unit that has Declared a Charge towards the unit that fled may take a Command Test; a Redirect Test (see the Psychology chapter). If the test is passed, the unit may immediately Declare a new Charge towards another unit (following all the usual restrictions for Declaring Charges). Each unit may only attempt to Redirect a Charge once per Phase.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: An Attachable Model in a Combined Unit may Declare a Charge on its own during the Charge Phase, i.e. Charging out of the unit and leaving the unit behind. When doing this, apply the following rules: • Use the position of the Combined Unit for determining which Facing of the enemy unit the Charge is Declared towards, and for determining the Flee direction if the Charged unit performs a Flee! Charge Reaction. • Use the Attachable Model for determining Line of Sight and distance to the enemy unit. • Attachable Models ignore the Unit Spacing rule with regards to the unit they are leaving. • The unit itself (including other Attachable Models in the unit) cannot Declare Charges in the same Player Turn. • If the Charge is successful, move the Attachable Model out of the unit by Charging as normal. If there is not enough room to physically move the model out of the unit, the Charge cannot be Declared. • If the Charge is not successful, the Attachable Model makes a Failed Charge Move out of the unit. If the Failed Charge Move is too short to place the Attachable Model outside 1" of the Combined Unit, the Attachable Model remains in the Combined Unit, and the entire Combined Unit performs the Failed Charge Move instead. • Once the Attachable Model Declares a Charge, it is treated as a separate unit. This means that the model uses its own Charge Speed.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Steady A unit is Steady if it has more Proper Ranks than each individual enemy unit Engaged in contact with it. If, at the end of a Round of Combat, the unit is Steady and was on the losing side, Discipline modifiers from the Combat Score difference are set to a minimum of -2 (i.e. cannot be a smaller number than -2). Solid A unit is Solid if its number of Proper Ranks is at least: • 4 – for units of Height 0-1. • 3 – for units of Height 2. • 2 – for units of Height 3-5. If a Height 1 unit is Solid at the start of a Round of Combat, then all Height 1 models in the unit gain Press of Ranks (+1 to wound, max. 3+) until the end of the Round of Combat. Steadfast If, at the end of a Round of Combat, the unit is both Steady and Solid, it is said to be Steadfast: modifiers to the unit’s Discipline from the Combat Score difference are ignored when rolling Break Tests. Always best to get the jump on the fuzz, not other way round. Need to be one step ahead in this game. Cannot just wait for them to get you – gotta seize the nishitive, or you’ll land yourself in the dungeons, and that in’t no fun at all. That’s what Klepa’s old witch-gaffa taught him, and that’s what Klepa would tell you if he weren’t upstanding honest pervayer of not-stolen goods. Surrounded A unit is considered Surrounded when it has enemies Engaged with either its Flank and/or Rear Facing. A Surrounded unit counts as having X fewer Proper Ranks, where X is the combined number of Proper Ranks of all the enemy units Engaged on its Flank and/or Rear. If multiple units in the same Combat are Surrounded, first apply Surrounded from units that are themselves not Surrounded. Then apply Surrounded from units that are Surrounded. The Active Player chooses the order in which to perform each of these steps. The primary effects of this are on the amount of Combat Score the unit will get for Proper Ranks (ie. Rank Bonus), and whether the unit and its enemies are Steady and/or Solid. Note that a unit that has 0 Proper Ranks would be unaffected by this reduction.

sharedProfiles.name: Choose a unit and a target

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: During the Shooting Phase, units containing Shooting Weapons or relevant Model Rules can perform Shooting Attacks. Select a friendly unit as the Shooting unit and an enemy unit as the Target unit (for further details, see Allocating Attacks in the Attacks chapter). • Shooting unit: to be eligible to shoot, a unit must not: • Be Shaken, • Be Engaged in Combat, • Have performed a Failed Charge Move this Player Turn, • Have made a March Move this Player Turn (unless it has March and Shoot), or • Already used its Shooting Attack this Player Turn. • Target unit: to be eligible to be shot at, a unit must: • Be within the Shooting unit’s Line of Sight, and • Not be Engaged in Combat.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Many models have choices that are determined in this step of the Round of Combat Sequence. Common ones: Make Way for Characters, Activate items and abilities and choose weapon. If both players have choices to do in this step, the Active Player first makes and executes all their choices, then the Reactive Player makes and executes all their own choices. Choose Melee Weapon Model parts armed with multiple weapons must choose which weapon to use in their First Round of Combat, with the following priority order*: • An Enchanted Weapon • Any weapon that is neither a Hand Weapon, nor an Innate Weapon • A Hand Weapon • An Innate Weapon *A model part with Weapon Master may choose what Melee Weapon to use in each Round of Combat, and only needs to conform to the Priority #1 hereabove.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: After all Fleeing and Pursuing units have been moved, any unit that is still Engaged in the Combat may attempt to perform a Combat Reform, with the following restrictions: • A unit Engaged on more than one of its Facings can never make a Combat Reform. • Any unit on the losing side of the Round of Combat, as well as any unit Engaged on its Flank or Rear Facing, must pass a Command Test to be able to Combat Reform. First, the Active Player declares which of their units will attempt to perform a Combat Reform, taking Command Test where needed. Then the Reactive Player declares which of their units will attempt to perform a Combat Reform, taking Command Test where needed. Any units that are not perfectly aligned with the Target Facing of an enemy they are Engaged with at the time of declaring which units will attempt a Combat Reform, must attempt to do so, following the usual rules for Combat Reforms. Once it has been established which units will perform a Combat Reforms, the Active Player chooses which player performs all of their Combat Reforms first; each player chooses in which order to perform their own units’ Combat Reforms. When performing a Combat Reform, remove the unit from the Battlefield and place it back into contact with the enemy unit(s), following the rules below: • The unit can be placed in any viable formation, provided its number of files does not change by more than 1 . • At least as many models from both the reforming unit, and all units it was in contact with before the Combat Reform, must still be in contact with opposing models as before, but they do not have to be the same models. • Any Attachable Model, from either side, that was in contact with an enemy before the Combat Reform must remain in contact after the Combat Reform. • The unit can not move into contact with enemy units it was not in contact with before the Combat Reform. • The unit must maintain contact with the same enemy units as before the Combat Reform, and with the same Facings of those enemy units. • After having made its Combat Reform, the unit must be perfectly aligned against the enemy Facing it is Engaged with. If multiple units are performing Combat Reforms, then the requirements mentioned above must be fulfilled at the end of all Combat Reforms by the first player, and then again at the end of all Combat Reforms by the second player, rather than after each individual unit has made its own Combat Reform. Combat Reforms.a) At the end of a Round of Combat, unit A is Engaged with unit B and Unit C. Unit A performs a Combat Reform. b) Unit A has made its Combat Reform: the unit has added a file on its right flank, and the Character joined to the unit has changed position so as to be located on its front-right corner.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When more than one unit has Declared a Charge towards the same enemy unit, the Charging units are moved in a slightly different order. • Roll Charge Range for each unit Charging that same target before moving any of them. • Decide the order that the units will be moved, both Charge Moves and Failed Charge Moves. This must be chosen so that the number of units that successfully completes a Charge is as high as possible. • Move the units, one by one, following the normal Charge Move rules with the following exceptions: • Never apply the rules for Unaligned Charges or Blocked Path. If it is not possible to place the Charging Unit fully aligned with the enemy, the Charge is not possible. • Each individual unit is not required to maximize the number of models in contact (conditions 3 and 4). The conditions are instead applied at the end of all the Charge Moves. This means that the total number of models from both sides are maximised after all successful Charges have been resolved. • In situations where not all the Charging Units can complete their Charge Move, e.g. due to other units blocking the path, such units will instead perform a Failed Charge Move.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Attachable Models that join other units form a Combined Unit. Once an Attachable Model has joined a unit, they are considered part of the unit for all rules purposes, unless specified otherwise.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Command Tests represent a warrior’s ability to perform orderly battlefield manoeuvres and rally after a rout has begun. Common situations where Command Tests are taken are: • When attempting to Redirect a Charge. Remember that this can only be attempted once per Phase per unit. • When attempting to perform a Combat Reform while on the losing side, and/or when Engaged on the Flank or Rear. • When taking a Rally Test. See the Rally Phase chapter for details. Common Model Rules that affect Command Tests are: Disciplined,Mindless, Commanding Presence, Unruly (see Model Rules for details). Panic? Klepa is always cool as coocumber. What’s the secret to staying calm? Just remember: you are an honest goblin with a pure heart, nothing to hide, and lots of eemaculit alibis.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: All Leaders gain Commanding Presence (6"). The Discipline of all models within X" of a friendly non-Knocked Down, non-Hidden model with Commanding Presence may be set to the Discipline value of that model, where X is given within the brackets of the Model Rule (this ability follows the normal rules for Priority of Modifiers, page priorityOfModifiers, meaning that effects modifying the Discipline of the model with Commanding Presence are applied before setting the recipient model’s Discipline to that value; this value may then be further modified). If X is given as a modifier (e.g. +6"), the Universal Rule gains this as a modifier to its range. If the model doesn’t have the Universal Rule, the range is set to this value.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: To help with playing The 9th Age, we have a continually updated list of Community Tools. These are all found on the T9A Download page and are free to use. The most popular one at the release of 3.0 (and for a long time before then) is the online army builder tool New Recruit, developed by ‘Flammy’. New Recruit is updated directly from the internal 9th Age files, so its point calculations are generally correct and updated with hardly any delay. All tournament organisers are encouraged to use New Recruit, since the data collected from it are used by our teams to balance the game. This balancing includes (but is not limited to) determining which units are potentially too popular or remain underused. You can find it at this address: NewRecruit.eu All community tools are available for free here: https://community.the-ninth-age.com/wcf/downloads/#communitysupportmaterial.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Two objects, such as bases, Unit Boundaries, Terrain Features, and so on, are considered to be in contact if: • They touch one another: • Along a line (e.g. two rectangular bases contacting each other along their front). • At a single point (e.g. corner to corner contact between units). • One object is overlapping another. An object is considered to be inside another if it is either partially or fully inside that other object. Contact between Models and Units • Two or more units are in contact if their Unit Boundaries touch each other (including corner to corner contact). • Two or more models are in contact if their bases touch each other (including corner to corner contact, and including across empty gaps in a unit, see below). • A model is in contact with a unit if it is in contact with that Unit’s Boundary. Contact between Models across Gaps Incomplete ranks or Characters with Mismatching Base may cause gaps between opposing models whose units are in contact. Two opposing models are considered to be in contact with each other across such gaps if you can draw a straight line: • from one model to the other (including corner to corner), • that is perpendicular to both units’ Engaged Facings. A model is considered not to be in contact across a gap if its entire Facing that is opposite the enemy model is itself in contact with a friendly model.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Courage Tests represent a warrior’s ability to hold their position in the face of adversity. There are two primary types of Courage Tests: • Panic Tests: those tests are taken immediately when triggered by some circumstances. A unit that fails a Panic Test becomes Shaken. • Break Tests: taken by units on the losing side of a Combat (see the Melee Phase chapter for details). Common Model Rules that affect Courage Tests are: Beacon of Courage, Commanding Presence (see Model Rules for details). at (current page.south east) -1 ;

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A unit containing Courageous must reroll failed Courage Tests.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: For each model that is shooting, check if the target benefits from Cover by drawing three straight lines from the Shooting model to the target. These lines all start from the same point on the Shooting model’s base, as was used checking Line of Sight to the target. • One line is drawn to the right corner of the Target Facing. • One line is drawn to the left corner of the Target Facing. • One line is drawn to the centre of the Target Facing. If two or more of these lines pass through Obstructions that contribute to Cover (both Soft or Hard), the target benefits from Soft Cover. If at least two of these lines pass through Obstructions that contribute to Hard Cover, apply instead the rules for Hard Cover. Example of Cover in the Terrain Feature.The centre of the blue unit’s Front Facing is located in the red unit’s Flank Arc: the Flank Facing is the Target Facing. Two of three of the drawn lines pass through a Forest: the red unit benefits from Soft Cover. Obstructions that Contribute to Cover There are two types of Cover: Soft and Hard. The most common reason for applying Cover is the target being obscured by Terrain or other models, or the target being inside a Terrain Feature. The following Obstructions contribute to Cover: Soft Cover • Terrain that is Covering Terrain* and that contributes to Soft Cover. • Models that have equal or larger Height than either the shooter or the target. Hard Cover • Terrain that is Opaque Terrain • Terrain that is Covering Terrain* and that contributes to Hard Cover. • Models that have equal or larger Height than both the shooter and the target. *See the Terrain chapter for details. Note that models that have a smaller Height than both the shooter and the target do not contribute to Cover.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Covering Terrain contributes to Cover when drawing Line of Sight through it. The bracket (X) indicates whether the terrain contributes to Soft Cover or Hard Cover. Certain Terrain Features (such as Ruins, Fields) only count as Covering Terrain for units in contact with them. Ignore any Terrain Feature the shooter itself is located in for Cover purposes. Covering Terrain always has a bracket (Height Y) associated with it that corresponds to the largest Height where this Terrain Feature can contribute to Cover. For example, Fields are Covering Terrain (Height 3), which means that anything with Height 4-5 cannot claim Soft Cover from Line of Sight drawn through a Field they are in contact with. Sometimes terrain will have “Covering terrain (X) for units in contact”. This rule is meant to represent terrain that can be used for Cover, but is not tall enough to always provide it. Therefore, a unit needs to be close enough to benefit from it.

characteristics.name: Attack Attributes
characteristics.$text: Unwieldy (1)

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: When a model part with Crush Attack allocates its attacks in Combat, it may choose to exchange all of its Standard Melee Attacks for a single Standard Melee Attack, which has its Strength and Armour Penetration both set to 10 and gains Multiple Wounds (D3). This cannot be done as a Restricted Attack.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A unit must take a Dangerous Terrain Test at the end of its move if it has been in contact with a Dangerous Terrain during one the following moves: Charge Move, Failed Charge Move, March Move, Flee Move, or Pursue Move. Dangerous Terrain Tests are performed by rolling a number of D6. For each roll of X+, the unit suffers a hit that wounds automatically with always AP 10. (Note: Special Saves can still be taken, and this is not an attack). The number of dice the unit must roll is equal to half the number of models in it (rounding fractions up), multiplied by the models’ Height. If a value is given for Y, only models fulfilling these criteria take the Dangerous Terrain Test. For example, a unit of 19 Height 1 Dwarven Warriors would roll 10 dice (19÷2 –> 10, ×1), while a unit of a single Height 5 Dragon would roll 5 dice (1÷2 –> 1, ×5). If one of the above-mentioned moves was performed by a Unit that has been in contact with several Terrain Features that are Dangerous Terrain, every Health Pool it contains must make a Dangerous Terrain Test for each Terrain Feature with Dangerous Terrain it has been in contact with, one at a time, removing any casualties caused by the first test before calculating the number of dice that must be rolled for the next test. If a type of model is indicated in the brackets (Y), any model not fulfilling this criteria is considered Height 0 for Dangerous Terrain Test purposes. • Only Health Pools that have actually been in contact with a Dangerous Terrain Feature need to roll any Dangerous Terrain Test. • Calculate the number of Dangerous Terrain Tests to roll for each Health Pool that has been in contact with the Terrain Feature, and roll the tests separately. The damage from each test is allocated towards the Health Pool that the test was rolled for. For example, a unit of 10 Orc Warriors (Rank-and-File models, Height 1 ) is joined by two Orc Characters on Grunter (Height 2). If the unit moves through Dangerous Terrain in such a way that one of the Characters never touches the Terrain Feature, the Dangerous Terrain Tests are rolled in the following way: 5 dice for the Rank-and-File Health Pool (10÷2, ×1), 2 dice for the one Character that came in contact with the Terrain Feature (1÷2 –> 1, ×2), and no test for the other Character.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Before building an army, players need to agree on the scale of the battle, which corresponds to the chosen Army Size. Armies are then built so that the combined point costs of all their units does not exceed the designated Army Size, and is no less than than 50 points below that limit. Army Size also determines the rules for army composition. Points Cost The Points Cost, often shortened pts, is a measure of the power of a unit or upgrade. We use points to ensure that two armies with a similar total Points Cost facing each other provide for a fair, balanced game experience. Every unit has a Points Cost, which is determined by adding its base cost with the cost of additional models added to it, as well as the cost of every additional option selected for that unit.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A model is Decimated when its original* unit’s current Health Points is 25% or less of its starting Health Points, as listed in the Army List. Decimated models are removed as casualties just before they would perform a Flee Move. * By original unit, it is meant the unit as listed on the Army List. This means that the Rank-and-File part of a Combined Unit might be considered Decimated while an Attachable Model joined to the unit is not, or vice versa. In this case, remove only Decimated models from the unit before performing a Flee Move, and leave models that are not Decimated on the Battlefield.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: To Declare a Charge, select one of your units that has not already Declared a Charge this Phase, and that is not Engaged in Combat or Shaken. Declare which enemy unit it will try to Charge, that fulfil all the following conditions: • The enemy unit must be in Line of Sight* of the Charging Unit. • It must be possible to complete the Charge towards the enemy unit. I.e. the enemy unit must be within the Charging Unit’s maximum potential Charge Range, and there must be enough room to move the Charging Unit into Contact*. *Line of Sight and Contact are both defined in the Definitions and Terminology chapter. Only consider effects affecting the Charging Unit’s Charge Range that are present when the Charge is declared. When determining if there is enough room for the Charging Unit, take into account already declared Charges, including Initial Align Moves of Charging Units. Do not consider Flee! Charge Reactions, or potential casualties inflicted on the units. Once a Charge is declared, the unit is considered to be Charging until one of the following occurs: • It has finished its First Round of Combat after making a Charge Move. • It performs a Failed Charge Move. • It is not Engaged in Combat. So you’re getting charged. You screwed the pooch. You know the position you got yourself in is wrong. The question is, what’re you gonna do about it? There’s an old saying among us goblins, real pearl of wisdom, what I would transeeliorate as “Always better to run away.” You know who doesn’t know that saying? Dead people. I mean lititerally! Those shufflers and groaners just don’t care. They’re already dead, see? What have they got to worry about? Something happens to them, they can just get back up again. That’s why you’ll never see a zombie running away from a fight. Same goes for the spawn of the netherworld. Your average daemon don’t mind kicking the bucket, they only get poofed back into the other Realm. So they ain’t running scared neither. Course, being so nonch-allont about dying makes them even scarier for those of us who still have to bother about such cares and concerns. So you listen to your goblin pal: Always run away.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The Defender chooses a Deployment Zone. This determines which side of the battlefield each army will start the game. The Defender then performs all their Pre-game Selections

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each model has four Defensive Characteristics. These Characteristics are common for all model parts on the same model. 1whiteblack!5 Abbreviation & Characteristics name & Description HP & Health Points & A model is removed as a casualty when it loses this many Health Points. Def & Defensive Skill & How well the model avoids being hit in melee. Res & Resilience & How easily the model withstands blows. Arm & Armour & A high Armour value means the model is able to deflect wounds that should have put it out of Combat.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Some rules may be triggered by a unit performing a Move, which is one of the following actions: • Move Manoeuvres (Advance Move, March Move, Reform Move) and any rule that refers to any of these, such as Vanguard Moves and Magical Moves. • Charge Move (including the Align Move) and Failed Charge Move. • Flee Move and Pursue Move (including Overrun, and Random Movement). • Combat Reform and Post-combat Pivot.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Starting with the Attacker, players then take turns Deploying their units fully inside their own Deployment Zone. All units must follow the Unit Spacing rule (defined in the Definitions and Terminology chapter). On each of their Deployment Turns, a player can Deploy any number of units, and must Deploy at least one unit. Any Attachable Model that wishes to begin the game joined to a unit must be Deployed inside and simultaneously with that unit. Once a player has Deployed their entire army, that player immediately chooses who has the first Player Turn. Note: this entire army criteria does not include units that can, and choose to, be Deployed later during the game (such as units entirely with Ambush, Hidden). Since finishing Deployment first allows you to choose which player has the first Player Turn, a common practice is to Deploy your entire army the first chance you get. Once your are more comfortable with the game, you will start weighing the strategic benefits from knowing where the opponent’s troops are Deployed against the advantage of choosing who has the first Player Turn. Rules and Abilities of Undeployed Units Until being Deployed, units cannot perform any actions at all, and all their Magic Items, rules, and abilities not related to their Deployment are ignored, unless explicitly stated otherwise. Undeployable Units In the unlikely event that a unit cannot be Deployed during the Deployment Phase for whatever reason (e.g. if there is not enough space in the player’s Deployment Zone), it is removed as a casualty, unless specifically stated otherwise.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The order in which Melee Attacks are performed is determined before any attacks take place. This order is known as the Agility Order and is based on the Agility of the attacking model parts. The highest Agility attacks are resolved first, followed by lower Agility attacks. Once the Agility Order is determined, it remains so for the entire Round of Combat. Charging Momentum Charging models gain +1 Agility.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: If no outside source tells you what Deployment Type to use, players can use the Frontline Clash standard Deployment Type, or choose one from the Season Pack. Frontline Clash The Central Line is the line drawn through the centre of the board and parallel to the Long Battlefield Edges. Deployment Zones are more than 12" away from the Central Line, towards your Long Battlefield Edge, and more than 6" from the Short Battlefield Edges. frontlineclash

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The Victory Conditions for the game are divided into three parts (see chapter After the Game for their relative importance): • Victory Points, representing how much of the opponent’s army has been removed as a casualty. • A single Primary Objective, that both players compete to win. • If using Secondary Objectives, one for each player see the Season Pack; if this is your first game, we recommend playing without Secondary Objectives. If no outside source (e.g. tournament organiser, campaign rule, Season Packs…) tells you which Primary Objective to use, use the one below. Scoring Units Any Rank-and-File unit that fulfils all the conditions below is a Scoring Unit: • It has a Standard Bearer. • It does not have Light Troops. • It was not Summoned during the game. • It did not arrive on the Battlefield in Game Turn 6 (e.g. via Ambush). A unit that is Shaken (see the Psychology chapter) temporarily stops being Scoring until it is no longer Shaken. Rank-and-File Units Any unit containing at least one Rank-and-File model (see Models and Units in the Definitions and Terminology chapter) is a Rank-and-File unit. Primary Objective – Hold the Centre Setup during Determine and Setup Primary Objective: mark the Battlefield Centre. Rules: END of Game Turns 3 to 6, the player with the most Scoring units within 9" of the Battlefield Centre gains a single Objective Counter. End of Game Completion: the player with the most Objective Counters wins.

sharedProfiles.name: Determine who Flees and who Pursues

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: If any unit failed its Break Test or was wiped out during the Combat, follow the steps below in order: 1 & Determine Flee Direction: each Broken unit (i.e. any unit that failed its Break Test) will Flee away from an enemy unit it is in contact with. If there are more than one unit to Flee away from, the owner of those enemy units chooses which is used to establish the Flee direction. 2 & Roll Flee Distance: typically, this is a roll of 1d6+4. Place the resulting dice next to the unit, but do not move the unit yet. 3 & Determine which units will Pursue: each unit in contact with one or more Broken enemy units, and no non-Broken enemy units, may choose to Pursue. Declare which unit is Pursuing which Broken unit. • A unit that was Charging in the previous Round of Combat and is now no longer in contact with any enemy unit (usually, because all of them have been wiped out) may choose to perform a special type of Pursuit called an Overrun. An Overrun is always straight forward. 4 & Roll Pursue Distance: typically, this is a roll of 1d6+4. Place the resulting dice next to the unit, but do not move the unit yet. 5 & Remove caught Broken units: compare the Flee Distance of each Broken unit with the Pursue Distances of any unit that Declared a Pursuit towards it. If the Flee Distance is greater than all Pursue Distances, the Broken unit managed to get away. Otherwise, the unit was caught and is removed as a casualty.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Some attacks require a to-hit roll, while other attacks hit automatically, inflicting a fixed or random number of hits. The rules for how attacks hit are described for each attack. The most common type of to-hit rolls can be found in the Shooting Phase and Melee Phase chapters. Whenever an effect inflicts a random number of hits on more than one unit, roll for the number of hits separately for each unit, unless specifically stated otherwise.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: A Charging model with this Attribute, or using a weapon with this Attribute, gains the Model Rules and Characteristic modifiers stated in brackets (X). For example, a Charging model part with Devastating Charge (+1 Strength, Poison Attacks) gains +1 Strength and Poison Attacks when it is Charging. This rule is cumulative: a model part with several instances of Devastating Charge applies all Attack Attributes and Characteristics modifiers from all of them when Charging.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: This game uses six-sided dice for determining random outcomes. These dice are referred to as a D6. The following different types dice rolls are used in the game: • Specific Value: when the result depends on whether the rolled value meets a specific value, this is noted with single quotation marks around the value, such as ‘1’. • Higher or Equal to: when the result depends on rolling equal to or higher than a specific target, this is written with a plus sign, such as 3+, meaning 3 or higher. • Multiple Dice: sometimes multiple dice are rolled together and, unless stated otherwise, their results are added together. This is indicated by a number preceding the dice type, such as 3D6, meaning roll three dice and add their results together (for an end result of 3 to 18). • Modified Dice Rolls: dice rolls can be modified in the following ways: • Adding a number, e.g. D6+2 • Subtracting a number, e.g. D6-2 • Multiplying with a number, e.g. D6×2 • Maximised and Minimised Roll: for each instance of Maximised or Minimised, roll an additional dice, and discard the lowest or highest rolled dice before applying modifiers or adding any results. • Maximised: for each instance of Maximised, add a dice to the roll, and discard the dice that rolled the lowest result. • Minimised: for each instance of Minimised, add a dice to the roll, and discard the dice that rolled the highest result. • Both: if both Maximised and Minimised are applied to the same roll, each instance of one cancels out an instance of the other. • Rerolling Dice: certain effects allow for rerolling specific dice once. This means picking up the dice that meet the reroll criteria and rolling them again, with the second result being final (i.e. a rerolled dice can never be rerolled again). • Rolling a D3: a D3 is a three-sided dice that will yield a result between 1 and 3. This can be simulated by halving the result of a D6 roll, rounding up (ie. ‘1’ and ‘2’ on a D6 count as 1; ‘3’ and ‘4’ on a D6 count as 2; ‘5’ and ‘6’ on a D6 count as 3).

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: When an attack with Direct Hit hits, after determining the number of hits (e.g. in the case of Area Attack), a single hit, chosen by the attacker, gains the Rules and Characteristic modifiers stated in brackets. If a Strength and/or Armour Penetration is given directly, set the attack’s Strength and/or Armour Penetration to that value (for example, Direct Hit (Str 10, AP 6) means one hit from that attack has its Strength set to 10 and its Armour Penetration set to 6 .

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Command Tests taken by a unit containing Disciplined benefit from Minimised.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Units in contact with a Disruptive Terrain cannot claim Combat Score bonus from their number of Proper Ranks (i.e. Rank Bonus).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Close Combat Attacks allocated towards a model with Distracting suffer a -1 to-hit modifier. This to-hit modifier cannot be combined with any other negative to-hit modifiers.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: Successful Aegis Saves taken against the attack must be rerolled.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: All Cosmology spells are divided into two versions, representing opposing aspects: Cosmos and Chaos . When casting a Cosmology spell, always declare which version of the spell you are using, and substitute the square brackets ([𝛼]) with the content listed in the table at the bottom of each Spell Card corresponding to the chosen version (Cosmos or Chaos).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Most Model Rules are not cumulative. This means that if a model or a model part gains the same rule multiple times, the effects do not stack or provide extra benefits. This includes Model Rules with different keywords attached (such as Multiple Wounds (towards Height 2) and Multiple Wounds (towards Height 3)), which are considered to be the same Model Rule, meaning that both instances cannot be applied simultaneously. In such cases, the owner may choose which instance of the Model Rule to use at any time.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Certain abilities may provide time-limited additional effects to models. Generally such effects immediately cease to work when a model is removed. The following key-words are used to denote the durations of such effects. • Instant: the effects are applied once, then immediately end. • Round of Combat: the effects last until the end of the Round of Combat in which they were applied. • One Phase: the effects last until the end of the Phase in which they were applied. • End of Combat: the effects last until the model is Unengaged. • End of Turn: the effects last until the end of the Player Turn in which they were applied. • One Turn: the effects last until the start of the next same Phase as when the effects were applied, of the same player (e.g if the effects were applied during the Magic Phase of Player A, then they end at the start of the next Magic Phase of Player A.) • Permanent: the effects last until the end of the game, or until a specific condition is met as described in the effect. Permanent effects do not end when if the model applying the effect is removed as a casualty. • One use only: these effects can only be used once per game. Each One use only effect will describe when it can be used (or activated). -1 Extended Effects and Combined Units It can happen that a unit affected by effects with an extended duration (such as One Turn or Permanent) becomes divided into multiple units – the most common example of this is when an Attachable Model leaves the unit that it was joined to. When this happens, the effects keep applying to each of those elements for the given duration. See Attachable Models chapter for Continuous effects. An Attachable Model who joins a unit affected by an effect, or a unit that is joined by an Attachable Model affected by an effect, do not become affected themselves. Simultaneous Effects When multiple effects occur at the same time, the Active Player resolves their effects first. Each player decides the order in which they resolve their own simultaneous effects.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When a model with Dying Blow is about to be removed as a casualty during any Agility Step of a Round of Combat it is fighting, remove it instead at the end of Agility Step 0.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: While wielding a Great Weapon, the model will strike at -1 Agility instead of always at Agility 0. When subject to the effects of Charging Momentum, the model will therefore strike at Agility 9.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Units entirely with Emplacement cannot Declare Charges, perform March Moves or Pursue Moves (including as part of a Random Movement), or choose the Flee! Charge Reaction. If a unit entirely with Emplacement is about to perform a Flee Move, it is instead removed as a casualty. The model cannot shoot in the same Player Turn that it has performed a Move Manoeuvre. Units entirely with Emplacement can draw Line of Sight in any direction from any points on their base (i.e. they are not limited by their Front Facing or Front Arc). When determining facing it is shooting towards, measure from the centre of model with Emplacement´s base, instead of its Front Facing.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Once a unit completes a Charge Move, the Charging Unit and the target unit are Engaged in Combat, and remain Engaged in Combat as long as, at least their Unit Boundaries, are in contact with an enemy Unit Boundary.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Once during each Shooting Phase, a non- Shaken and Unengaged model with Engineer can select a friendly model with X in a unit within 6": the selected model gains +1 to hit with Shooting Attacks, to a maximum of 3+. No model can be affected by more than one instance of this effect simultaneously. The use of this rule must be declared before shooting with the selected model.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The wearer’s Armour is set to 5 and can never be improved beyond this.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: After both Siphon the Veil and Storing Magic, if a player has more than twice the number of Magic Dice in his pool than the number gained from the Flux Card, the player must discard each Magic Dice over this limit. For example, Flux Card XI grants 6 Magic Dice: it sets the Excess Magic limit to a maximum of 12 Magic Dice.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: This rule limits which units an Attachable Model is allowed to join. • Attachable Models with Exclusive (X) can only join units containing X. • Non-Attachable Models with Exclusive (X) can only be joined by Attachable Models with X. • If a unit has multiple instances of Exclusive, all criteria must be fulfilled together. The specific criteria for X can be unit names, Model Rules, Properties, upgrades, etc. If a model has both Exclusive and Attached, apply all requirements from both rules (remember that a model that cannot be Deployed is considered a casualty).

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: A model part with Extra Support replaces the limit on the maximum number of attacks the model can do as Restricted Attack with the value in brackets (X) or, if it includes a +, increases that limit with +X.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Failed Charge Move occurs when a unit cannot complete its Charge (e.g., due to an insufficient Charge Range, or due to obstacles making it impossible to complete the Charge Move). The Failed Charge Distance is always 4". If a unit suffers casualties during the Charge Move and therefore no longer can complete the Charge, the unit is also considered to have failed its Charge. The unit’s movement is then backtracked to the position it had when declaring the Charge Move, then it performs a Failed Charge Move. A Failed Charge Move is done by performing a Snaking Forward Move (see Manoeuvre Types in the Movement Phase chapter) with the following adjustments: • Initial Forward move is always 0". (i.e. a Failed Charge Move starts with a Wheel.) • Wheel towards the intended target until one of the following occurs: • The unit is facing the direction where a forward move would bring the centre of the Charging Unit straight towards the centre of the Target Facing, • The Wheel is 90 degrees. • The Wheeled distance is equal to the Failed Charge Distance. • The unit is about to come into contact with another unit or Impassable Terrain. Stop just before moving into contact. • Concluding Forward move until one of the following occurs: • The unit has moved a total distance (Wheel + Forward Move) equal to the Failed Charge Distance (4"). • The unit is about to come into contact with another unit or Impassable Terrain. Stop just before moving into contact. A unit that has performed a Failed Charge Move cannot perform any Move Manoeuvres in the same Player Turn, and it cannot shoot in the next Shooting Phase. If the target was removed as a casualty, perform the Failed Charge Move towards the last position of the centre of the Target Facing. Failed Charge Moves are allowed to end the move within 1" of Impassable Terrain or other units, but are not allowed to move into contact.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Models that are Fearless are immune to the effects of Fear.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The first time in each Charge Phase when an enemy model declares a Charge against this model, before the Charge has been plotted, it may perform a Retreat Move, provided it is not Engaged in Combat. To perform a Retreat Move, the model may be moved up to D6". Climbing, Jumping and Hiding may not be performed during a Retreat Move. After the Retreat Move has been performed, the Charging model gains Hatred until the end of the Player Turn and carries on with the Charge as normal, even if the target model moved out of Line of Sight. If the target model moves out of the maximum Charge Range of the Charging model, the Charge is cancelled. The Charging model may not perform another Charge in this phase, but otherwise does not count as Charging for the remainder of the Player Turn.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Fields can be represented in the game for example by meadows of tall grass, or agricultural enclosures. Fields have the following rules: Covering Terrain (Soft Cover, Height 3) for units in contact.# Flammable: units in contact gain Weakness (Flaming Attacks).

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: A model part with Fight in Extra Rank, or using a weapon with Fight in Extra Rank, can make Supporting Attacks from one additional rank.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: During its First Round of Combat, any model part with First Strike, or using a weapon with First Strike, gains the Rules and Characteristic modifiers stated in brackets. For example, a model part with First Strike (+1 Str) gains +1 Str in its First Round of Combat.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: The attack ignores Fortitude Saves and must reroll failed to-wound rolls against models with Flammable. At the end of an Advance Move, a model with Flaming Attacks can attempt to set on fire a Combustible Terrain Feature within 1". If a model chooses to do so, roll a D6. If the result is equal to or higher than X, where X is the number written within brackets of the Combustible keyword of the Terrain Feature, that Terrain Feature is now Burning. The model cannot perform any other Voluntary Actions in this Player Turn. If any attack with Flaming Attacks is directed at a model inside or on top of a Combustible Terrain Feature, roll 2D6 at the end of the phase. If both dice show a result that is equal to or higher than X, where X is the number written within brackets of the Combustible keyword of the Terrain Feature, that Terrain Feature is now Burning.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Flee Move is a specific type of move performed in certain situations. Common instances are: failing a Rally Test, choosing to Flee! as a Charge Reaction or failing a Break Test (without being caught by any Pursuing enemy unit). When making a Flee Move, follow these steps: 1 & Roll the Flee Distance (normally this is 1D6+4"). 2 & Each Flee Move starts by Pivoting the unit to face a certain direction, determined as such: • Failed Rally Test: Pivot the unit to face directly away from the closest non- Shaken enemy unit. The direction is specified by a line from Centre of unit to Centre of unit. If there are multiple enemy units at equal distances, the opponent chooses which one of its units will be used to determine the direction of the Flee Move. • Flee! Charge Reaction and failed Terror Tests: Pivot the unit to face directly away from the Charging enemy unit. The direction is specified by a line from Centre of unit to Centre of unit. • Failed Break Test: Pivot the Shaken unit so that its Rear Facing is parallel with the Facing of the enemy it was Engaged with. If multiple units are eligible, the opponent chooses which of their units will be used to determine the direction of the Flee Move. 3 & Move the Shaken unit straight forward by the distance rolled. 4 & A Flee Move, including the initial Pivot, ignores the Unit Spacing rule, and can move through any Obstructions. The move still cannot end with the Fleeing unit overlapping any other unit or Impassable Terrain: continue the move in a straight line until the unit can be placed on the battlefield without overlapping any Obstructions. Remember that the unit ignores the Unit Spacing rule, which means it can be placed within 1" of other units or Impassable Terrain. • If the Fleeing unit moves through any friendly unit, this unit must take a Panic Test. • If the Fleeing unit moves through any enemy unit or Impassable Terrain, treat these as Dangerous Terrain (4+). 5 & If the Flee Move brings the unit into contact with the Table Edge, or with an enemy unit that has declared a Charge against it during the same phase, the unit is removed as a casualty.

characteristics.$text: Models with Fly may use Flying Movement during Charge Moves, Advance Moves, and March Moves. During Flying Movement, the model cannot Jump or Climb. During Flying Movement, the model can move from point to point, any number of times during Advance and March Moves, and once during Charge Moves. When moving from point to point, the following applies: • The points can be suspended in mid air, provided the model ends the move on a Floor. • The model must be able to trace Line of Sight to itself on the new point from the current point. • The model must be able to move to the new point without moving into terrain or other models. • If a point to point movement moves the model directly beneath an Upper Level, it must take a Dangerous Terrain Test with Dangerous Terrain (2). This can be applied multiple times during a single move, once for each time a point to point movement is made. • When measuring the distance moved, measure horizontally if the new point is as high as or below the current position. Otherwise, measure directly.

characteristics.$text: When resolving a Round of Combat, the Unit Boundaries of the Engaged units are not updated, but retain their sizes and positions. Furthermore, the placement of models in those units is also not changed (e.g. to ensure viable formation when casualties are suffered). When calculating the number of ranks, files, or Proper Ranks a unit has (this is primality relevant for Steady and Solid, empty gaps in the unit formation (e.g. due to a dead Attachable Model) are considered to be filled in by models from back ranks, in the same way you would normally fill empty gaps (see the Definitions and Terminology chapter for details). Note that models are not physically moved at this stage. Unit Boundaries remain Frozen until just before Broken units perform their Flee Moves or when the unit whose boundary it is, is removed as a casualty. Note that the number of Proper Ranks can still be reduced for Steady or Solid purposes if models get removed during Combat. Unit Boundaries and models’ positions are Frozen in place, in order to prevent the need to do any finicky movement and repositions in messy situations, at a time where players should be focusing on rolling their attacks.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: At the start of the Charge Phase, each of your models with this rule that could declare a Frenzied Charge must take a Discipline Test, called a Frenzy Test. A Frenzied Charge follows all the normal rules for charges, with the following exceptions: • The Model cannot Jump during the Charge Move. • The target must be within Line of Sight. • The target must be reachable with a move needing a Charge Roll of 7. • The move must be plotted along the shortest possible route. If the Charge Range is insufficient, any Failed Charge Move is performed as normal. If there are no targets for a Frenzied Charge, the model may act as normal (including declaring a normal Charge).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Attachable Models can join other units either by Deploying inside and simultaneously with the unit, or by moving into contact with the unit through a Move Manoeuvre. Upon joining a unit, the unit that was joined cannot move further in the same Phase. A Attachable Model ignores the Unit Spacing rule with regards to the unit it is about to join, and must have enough movement to reach its final and valid position within the unit, which normally means it must be able to reach its Front rank. During the Player Turn in which an Attachable Model joins the unit, the Attachable Model and the unit are treated individually for the purpose of determining which model has moved or performed a March Move or not. Units that are Shaken or Engaged in Combat cannot be joined by an Attachable Model. The Attachable Model can choose any valid position it can reach with its move. This includes moving through the unit it joins, maybe displacing other Attachable Models. Displaced Rank-and-File models are placed in rear ranks. If the unit has a single rank, the Attachable Model or the displaced models can alternatively be placed on the side of the unit, forming a new file.

characteristics.$text: Upon resolving the effects of a Thaumaturgy spell Spell Effects (5.A Casting Spells, 6), first roll a D6 and apply the corresponding effect (if any) : • ‘5’ or ‘6’: apply the Blessing effect (marked with a ✠). • ‘1’: apply the Admonition effect (marked with a ×).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Model Rules include keywords to help define their effects. These keywords can be used directly within the Rulebook, and always apply to rules that have that keyword. Alternatively, keywords can be specified for individual rules on specific models, spells, or weapons. In this case, this is indicated within brackets following the name of the rule. List of Model Rule keywords: • Cumulative: effects from multiple instances of a Model Rule with the Cumulative keyword are combined and add up. • Distance Modifiers: written as a number followed by the " symbol. Any distance in the Model Rule description is replaced by that number. For example, Vanguard (3") means that the model can perform a Vanguard move, but its Mobility is set to 3 instead of the normal 6. • Shooting or Melee & Shooting: an Attack Attribute with the keyword Shooting only affects attacks that the model part makes with Shooting Weapons, while an Attack Attribute with the keyword Melee & Shooting affects both Melee Attacks and Shooting Attacks made by the model part. • Remember that the default if none of these keywords are used is that Attack Attributes only affect Melee Attacks. For example, by default, Poison Attacks only affect Melee Attacks. However, if a model part has Poison Attacks (Shooting), this means the Poison Attacks Model Rule only applies to attacks made with that model part’s Shooting Weapons, unless it also has Poison Attacks or Poison Attacks (Melee & Shooting). • Special Attacks: a model part with such a rule can make a special Melee Attack (which is not a Standard Melee Attack) that hits automatically. Since it is not a Standard Melee Attack, this attack can usually not be made as a Supporting Attack and does not suffer from Restricted Attacks (see the Melee Phase chapter). Special Attacks can be allocated onto any Attachable Model in units the attacker is Engaged in Combat with, if they are either or both: • Of a different Height than the Rank-and-File models in the unit. • In a unit with fewer than 5 Rank-and-File models (or fewer than 3 if they are of Height 3–5). • Towards X: the Attack Attribute only applies if the attack is allocated to a specific type of enemy model or an enemy model that has certain rules or Properties. The conditions are given as X. If more than one type of enemy is relevant, those types are separated by the word or. If multiple conditions must be fulfilled simultaneously, then they are separated by the word and. For example, Multiple Wounds (2, towards Height 4 and Beast, or Height 5) means that the rule Multiple Wounds is applied only when the attack is allocated either to a model that is both Height 4 and has the Property Beast, or to a model that is of Height 5, regardless of whether the model has the Property Beast. • Against X: the Model Rule only applies when the model is attacked by a certain type of model or by a model or attack with certain rules or Properties. For example, Hard Target (against Lethal Strike) means that the rule Hard Target applies only when the model is attacked by an attack with the Attribute Lethal Strike. See the rules under Towards X for how to interpret the words or and and. • Unique Keywords: in addition to the standard Model Rule keywords defined above, certain Model Rules have unique keywords. These are defined in their respective rules.

If, while doing a Reform Move Manoeuvre, its centre moves further than its Mobility, the move is considered a March Move for the purpose of rules triggered due to Marching (e.g. Dangerous Terrain Test and, if Undead, being restricted from performing a March Move, etc.). For the purpose of shooting, this is still a Reform Move. I.e. the unit can shoot if moving further than its Mobility. Note: this rule has no effect on other Move Manoeuvres, including March Moves.
