characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A model can draw Line of Sight to its target (a point, a model, or a Unit Boundary) if you can draw a line from the model to its target in the model’s Front Arc and without crossing Line of Sight-blocking Obstructions, such as: • Opaque Terrain (see the Terrain chapter). • Models in another unit whose Height is equal or greater than to both the model’s and its target’s. A model that is not in the front rank of a unit, instead draws its Line of Sight from a point on the Front Facing of its unit that is directly in front of it (typically from the Front Facing from a model directly in front of it). All of the following conditions must be fulfilled: • The line must be a straight line with its starting point on the model’s Front Facing. • The line can only deviate at most 45° from the straight forward direction of the model (this means that the line cannot be drawn outside the model’s own Front Arc). • Models never block Line of Sight to or from other models within the same unit. • The line between the model and the target does not cross over any Obstruction, such as: • Any Opaque Terrain. • The base of a model in another unit whose Height is equal or greater than both the model’s and its target’s. • A Unit Boundary whose Height is equal or greater than both the model’s and its target’s. A unit is considered to have Line of Sight to a target if at least one model in the unit can draw Line of Sight to it. For the purpose of drawing Line of Sight to or from a point on the Battlefield, that point is considered to be of Height 0. Drawing Line of Sight.The area within which the single model unit D can draw Line of Sight is marked. • Unit B is within Line of Sight. • Unit A is within Line of Sight, as unit D can draw Line of Sight to the Boundary of unit A, even though that part of A’s Unit Boundary is not occupied by any models. • Unit C is not within Line of Sight, as the Impassable Terrain Feature is an Opaque Terrain, therefore blocking Line of Sight from unit D to unit C.

characteristics.$text: When a model suffers an unsaved wound, it immediately loses a Health Point, which can result in models being removed as casualties. characteristics.$text: When a model loses its last Health Point, it is removed as a casualty. When the last model from a unit loses its last Health Point, the unit is removed as a casualty. Certain effects are triggered by models being removed as a casualty, while others are set off by models losing their last Health Point or reaching 0 Health Points. Losing the last Health Point does not apply to situations in which a model is directly removed as a casualty, without actually losing any Health Points (such as units leaving the Battlefield while doing a Flee Move, or being removed as a casualty after Breaking from Combat). Whenever a model that applies any effect to other elements in the game is removed as a casualty, unless specifically stated otherwise, that effect ends immediately. This also applies to effects that have a specified duration, such as activated effects with Duration: One Turn.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: In the Magic Phase, your Wizards will summon the magic swirling across the battlefield and use it to cast spells that blast the enemy or bolster your own forces – while your opponent tries to stop you. In the Magic Phase, your Wizards will summon the magic swirling across the battlefield and use it to cast spells that blast the enemy or bolster your own forces – while your opponent tries to stop you. Wizards are trained in one of the ten Paths of magic; their powers are limited by their own skill and by the availability of nearby magic, represented as Magic Dice. This store of power can be increased by channelling additional magic through the Veil – but be careful, for if you use too much magic to cast a spell, you run the risk of losing control! The Magic Phase is divided into the following steps: 1 & Draw Flux Card 2 & Siphon the Veil 3 & Store Magic Dice 4 & Apply Excess Magic 5 & Casting and Dispelling Spells: the Active Player attempts to cast a spell with one of their models; the Reactive Player may attempt to Dispel it. & Repeat step 5 for each spell you want to cast, or until out of Magic Dice.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Spells that are targeting at least one enemy model with Magic Resistance suffer a –X modifier to their Casting Attempts (where X is given in brackets). If there are different X values that could be used, use the highest value.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: The attack doesn’t have any special effects. However, it interacts with other rules, such as Aegis (X, against Magical Attacks). Model parts with Magical Attacks apply it also to their Special Attacks (such as Breath Attack and Impact Hits).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Some spells or abilities allow a unit to perform a Magical Move. This move is performed as if it were the Movement Phase, following the same rules and restrictions: the unit can perform a Move Manoeuvre. Characters and other Attachable Models can join or leave units. Restrictions that apply during the Movement Phase (e.g. units that are Shaken or Engaged in Combat cannot perform a Move Manoeuvre) still apply. The distance that the Magical Move can be performed is specified in the spell or ability. The target’s Mobility is changed to always equal to the distance of the Magical Move, for the duration of the move. For example, an effect could be: The target may perform a 6" Magical Move. This means the target can perform any normal Move Manoeuvre as if its Mobility was 6", including marching 12". A unit can only perform a single Magical Move per Phase.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Whenever there are gaps in the formation of a unit, or incomplete ranks other than in the rear rank of a unit, the unit’s formation must be reformed into a viable formation. Note: Except during a Round of Combat where Unit Boundaries and model placement in units are frozen. In this case, only follow the rules below when these are unfrozen. When redistributing models to fill gaps and incomplete ranks in the unit’s formation, do so in the following priority order: • Move models from the rear rank. • Move models from ranks other than the front rank. • Move models from the front rank. Avoid changing the number of files in the unit. If this is impossible (such as for a unit that only has a single rank), fill gaps by sliding all models from one side of the gap towards the other side. Maintaining a Viable Formation in Combat During a Round of Combat, the Unit Boundaries of all involved units are frozen, and models are not moved around inside the unit, not even to fill empty gaps inside their unit’s formation. This applies from the start of each Round of Combat, until just before moving Fleeing and Pursuing units. (See the Melee Phase chapter for details). When determining the number of ranks or files a unit has, gaps are considered filled by models in back ranks as normal, potentially reducing the actual number of ranks or files.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: It can happen that a Character’s unit is Engaged in Combat, while that Character is not itself in contact with any enemy model. When this happens, the Character may be eligible for a Make Way move. To be able to perform a Make Way move, the Character: • Must be in the first rank of its unit. • Must not be in contact with any enemy models. • Must not have a Mismatching Base. ̉ Make Way moves are performed when Choosing Equipment and Abilities. The Character switches positions with a Rank-and-File model (or models) in its unit that is in contact with an enemy. The Character must end up in a valid position. Normally this means that the Character can only swap positions with models in the Front rank.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Manoeuvre Types are different actions that can be made as part of other moves. For example, a Snaking Forward Move is used during Charge, Advance and March Moves, while Pivots are made during Advance Moves and Post-Combat Pivots. I know it might seem strange to think, but people who aren’t goblins sometimes like to move about in an organiferised fashion. Those sole-jers love nothing so much as marching up and down like lemmings with their perfect timing. What’s wrong with a good old crazed rush, I ask you, with everyone tripping over each other the way the gods intended? Some people just want to take the joy out of the mob.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: Marching in the same Player Turn while affected by this Attack Attribute does not prevent the attack from being performed, unless the attack is also subject to Move or Fire.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When performing a March Move, execute the following actions in the order given below: 1 & Snaking Forward Move (2×Mob): the unit may do any number of Snaking Forward Moves, with a total distance up to twice its Mobility (in inches). While performing these Snaking Forward Moves, the direction the unit is facing must stay within 90 degrees (in either direction) from the direction it was facing before the March Move. 2 & Reorder: models may be repositioned within the unit, as long as the number of files does not change.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: In Combined Units with both Attachable Models and Rank-and-File models, an Attachable Model is considered to have a Matching Base if the size of its base is the same as that of the Rank-and-File models in the unit, or if the size of its base is a multiple of the size of the Rank-and-File models’ bases in the unit. E.g. a 40×40 mm base in a unit where every model has a 20x20 mm base. Models on Matching Bases are placed inside the formation of the unit they join, normally displacing another model or models. If the model has a larger base than the Rank-and-File models, it counts as occupying all ranks its base covers for Proper Ranks calculations. -11.30tercioAngle.png If a model with a Matching Base has a longer base than the Rank-and-File models, it is possible that the unit finds itself with more than one incomplete rank, if all incomplete ranks consist entirely of models with such bases (e.g. the rear parts of long bases of models such as War Platform can form several incomplete ranks). A model cannot join a unit with more than one rank if its base is wider than the unit is, nor can a unit Reform into a formation narrower than any model joined to it.

characteristics.name: Rule

characteristics.$text: Distances in The 9th Age: Skirmish Campaignsare measured in inches, 1 inch being equal to 2.54 cm. The game is normally played using 28 mm miniatures. At this scale, you may envision an inch representing roughly 1.5 metres in real life. In this case, a longbow’s 30" range translates to 45 metres. You can also draw inspiration from history, seeing 1" as 10 metres instead. This gives the longbow a range of 300 metres: a standard battlefield of 72×48" table would then represent a real life area of 720×480 m, or roughly 50 football pitches. In medieval times, this would represent a battlefield where two forces with soldiers numbering from a few hundred to several thousand could meet. The rules often refer to things being within a certain distance. When measuring distances, the closest points between objects are used, even if there are intervening elements. Models or units are considered within range if the distance between their closest points is less than or equal to the given range. Measurements are taken from and to the Unit Boundary of a unit (i.e. not necessarily the actual models). Players are free to measure any distance at any time. Range Some effects, such as spells or shooting weapons, have a Range value (X"). This means that the effect can target things up to X inches away on the battlefield. Models or units are considered to be within range if the distance between their closest points is less than or equal to the given Range. Long Range For shooting weapons, we define targets as being in Long Range if they are further away than half of the weapon’s Range (but still within the maximum Range). lineskip Playing The 9th Age at different scales lineskip This game is designed to be compatible with changes in scale. The most common way to use this alternative mode of play is to play it at half-scale, where all distances are halved. This opens up possibilities for gameplay in more confined spaces, such as on ordinary kitchen tables, and entire armies can be neatly stored away in shoe boxes. • Distances: halve all measurements. This includes, but is not limited to, the battlefield dimensions, weapon and spell ranges, Mobility and Charge values, base sizes, area of effects, and more. Alternatively, you could decide to replace inches by centimetres (so that any distance of 10″ becomes 10 cm instead). • Models: use smaller models, designed to fit on the half base size. Typically, models suitable for this scale are in the 10 mm range. • Custom Measuring Devices: it is recommended that custom-made measuring devices are used, where all measurements are pre-halved. Such tools simplify rule referencing, eliminating the need for mental recalibration. Alternatively, if you have decided to replace inches by centimetres, you can measures all distances with a normal ruler, measuring centimetres instead of inches.

characteristics.$text: Some say that battles are won or lost by preparation or sound strategies, but ultimately every fight will come down to the clash of weapons in close quarters. The Melee Phase is the time for your forces to put their mettle to the test, once they have met the enemy in Combat, and discover whether their strength – and a touch of divine fortune – can bring them the victory. And perhaps more important, whether the defeated side can continue to fight on. This is also when your leaders and champions will meet in single Combat with their counterparts, fighting great duels that will live in legend. During the Melee Phase, all Engaged units will attack each other: each group of interlocked units in contact with each other is called a Combat. Each Combat goes through a Round of Combat, one Combat after another. Giants are a fascinating species, pseudo-symbiotic with other peoples, whose instinct for friendship has led them to become weapons of war throughout history. Some call this tragic, some call it noble. Today, with sixteen factions of growing strength locked in a delicate balance of power, certain bold, original, brilliant observers have hypothesised that perhaps it could be the trusting, suggestible giants that might tip the fragile equilibrium in favour of one group or another. You can find out more about this provocative, insightful idea in my latest three-volume masterwork, Giant By Name: How the World Underestimates Jotun Potential, available in all fine bookshops that stock self-published authors. The Melee Phase is carried out using the following sequence: I & Enemy Wiped. If a unit’s opponents have been removed outside the Melee Phase, the unit may perform a Post-Combat Pivot or an Overrun (if it was Charging). II & Round of Combat. Each Combat is resolved in an order chosen by the Active Player. For each Combat, follow this sequence: • Preparations for Combat • Remove Shaken units • Freeze Unit Boundaries • Combat Set-Up • Check Combat Formations • Static Combat Score • Combat Selections Choose Equipment and Abilities • Perform Melee Attacks • Determine Agility Order • Allocating Attacks • Resolve Attacks • Determine the Winner • Casualty-based Combat Score • Final Combat Score • Take Break Tests • Breaking and Pursuing • Determine who Flees and who Pursues • Unfreeze Unit Boundaries • Move Fleeing Units • Move Pursuing Units • Post Combat • Perform Post-Combat Pivots • Perform Combat Reforms III & Repeat steps II for each Combat: choose a Combat and complete all actions in the Round of Combat Sequence for each unit in that Combat, before moving on to resolve the next Combat. IV & Once all Combats have been resolved, the Melee Phase ends. Enemy Wiped Sometimes a unit that was previously Engaged in Combat had all its opponents removed before the start of the next Melee Phase. Such units follow the rules for No More Foes. If the unit has not moved since the enemy units were removed (e.g. with a Magical Move), it may perform a Post-Combat Pivot, or an the unit was considered Charging immediately before removing the enemy unit. Combat Each Combat is fought between a group of units that are in contact with each other. Most often, it involves only two opposing units Facing off, but it can also include multiple units against a single enemy unit, or a series of units from both sides all linked together. The Active Player chooses one such Combat to fight in a Round of Combat (which means all actions connected to a Round of Combat must be resolved with all Engaged units). Then the Active Player chooses a new Combat that has not been fought in this Melee Phase, to fight a Round of Combat. Continue choosing and resolving Combats until all of them has been fought. First Round of Combat During the First Round of Combat, specific rules come into play. A unit’s First Round of Combat occurs in two situations: • The First Round of Combat it fights after successfully Charging an enemy unit. • The First Round of Combat after it has been successfully charged by an enemy unit, whereas it was not already Engaged in Combat. Combined Combats Any Combat that involves more than two units is called a Combined Combat.

characteristics.$text: Any base that is not a Matching Base is considered a Mismatching Base, such as an Attachable Model on a 40×40 mm base in a unit where Rank-and-File models have 25×50 mm bases. A model with a Mismatching Base is always placed in contact to the side of the unit, aligned with its Front. Each unit can only include two models with Mismatching Bases, one on each side. These models are considered to be only in the Front rank, and are not counted when determining the number of models in each rank for Proper Ranks. They form a separate file of one model each. Matching and Mismatching Bases.a) A Character on a Mismatching Base is placed next to the unit. Characters on Matching Bases are placed inside the unit, as far forwards as possible. This unit is considered to have 6 files and 4 ranks. b) When an Attachable Model joins the unit, the small Attachable Model in the second rank must be moved to the side in order to have all Attachable Models as far forwards as possible.

characteristics.$text: Even though Model Rules are given to individual models, some of them function on a unit level, such as those dictating how entire units can move or operate. Model Rules differentiate between the following cases (The same keywords also apply to Properties): • Units entirely with X: whenever a Model Rule is referred to as units entirely with the rule, this refers to units where every single model in it has the Rule X or the Property X. • Units containing X: whenever a Model Rule is referred to as units containing the rule, this refers to units where at least one model in it has the Rule X or the Property X. • Units not containing X: whenever a Model Rule is referred to as units not containing the rule, this refers to units where no single model in it has the Rule X or the Property X.

characteristics.$text: In The 9th Age: Skirmish Campaigns, miniatures embody epic warriors, fierce monsters, and powerful spellcasters. Most warriors combine to form disciplined regiments called units, and several such units form the foundation of your army. Model A single gaming piece, placed on a base. Each model has its own profile, which consists of various characteristics values, model rules, and equipment. The profile reflects the capabilities of the model. Rank-and-File model Normal models in a unit. All models, except Attachable Models (such as all Characters), are referred to as Rank-and-File models. Base The platform on which a model rests. Bases are square or rectangular, and represent the area of the battlefield occupied by the model. In the game rules, the base is the only physical aspect of the model that matters. Bases are measured in [front-width × side-length], e.g., 25×50 mm for most horse riders. Unit A group of one or more models that operate as a single entity, arranged in a rectangular formation. Models in a unit move and fight together, coordinating their actions on the battlefield. When forming a unit of multiple models, the following conditions must be met to form a viable formation: • The models are placed in a tight rectangular (or square) formation, facing the same direction. • The unit cannot voluntarily have more ranks than files, unless the unit is wide enough to have a Proper Rank. • For units that are always considered to have 0 Proper Ranks, such as units entirely with Light Troops, apply this rule as if they could form Proper Ranks (e.g. a Height 1 unit entirely with Light Troops cannot have more ranks than files, unless it is at least five models wide). • Joining a unit with a Character or other Attachable model is a voluntary action. • The models are perfectly aligned and in contact with each other. • The width of the unit is determined by its first frontmost rank. No models may extend past this width. • Models not in the first rank must be positioned so that another model is directly in front of them, ensuring the entire front edge of their bases are in contact with the models in front of them. • All ranks within a unit must have the same width, except for the rear rank, which can be narrower. • It is acceptable for the rear rank to have gaps, as long as the models are aligned with those in the other ranks. • An Incomplete Rank refers to a rank with one or more missing models. When a rule, ability, spell, or any other effect affects a unit, all models of the unit are affected, unless explicitly stated otherwise. Unit Boundary The Unit Boundary is an imaginary rectangle encompassing the outer edges of a unit. A unit can never be inside the Boundary of another unit, unless they are explicitly allowed to temporarily be overlapping. (Unit Boundaries can be represented by using unit trays of the right dimensions.) Unit’s centre A unit’s centre is the centre of its Unit Boundary. Facings A unit or a model has four Facings, that correspond to the edges of the Unit Boundary or the model’s base: a Front, a Rear, and two Flanks. Arcs A unit’s Arcs correspond to the area in front of the four Facings, divided by a straight line extending from the corners of the Unit Boundary at a 135° angle from the unit’s Facings. Unit Arcs, Unit Facings, and Unit Boundariesa) This unit has 3 ranks and 5 files. The rear rank is incomplete and only contains 4 models. The Front, Flank, and Rear Arcs are defined by drawing lines from the corners of the Unit Boundary at a 135° angle from the unit’s Facings. b) The Unit Boundary is the area drawn around the outer edges of the unit (shaded red lines). The Centre of the unit is the centre of the Unit Boundary. c) A Unit Boundary cannot be inside another Unit Boundary, not even with parts that are not occupied by any models. Proper Ranks The number of models required to form a Proper Rank depends on the unit’s Height: • 5 models for Height 0-2. • 3 models for Height 3-4. • 1 model for Height 5. Ranks and Files Lines of models in the same unit that are side by side are called ranks. Lines of models that are directly in front of and behind each other are called files. Model Parts Some models have multiple lines of Offensive Profiles. Each line represents a different model part. For example, a cavalry model consists of two model parts: a rider and its mount. If a rule, ability, spell, or effect affects a model, then all its model parts are affected, unless stated otherwise. During attacks or shooting, each model part uses its own characteristics and weapons.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Modifiers can affect the values of Characteristics, dice rolls, or other numerical values in the game. They can set values, add or subtract from them, multiply or divide them, and are applied in the following order: • A Value Set to a Fixed Number: when a value or a roll is set to a specific number, replace the original value or roll with that number. When a value is set to at least a number, do not set the value if it would result in a reduction to the value. • Multiplication and Division: values or rolls can be multiplied or divided by a given number. • Addition and Subtraction: values or rolls can be modified by adding or subtracting a given number to or from them. • If a limit is defined in the rule, apply the modification after other operations that do not define a limit, and only up to that limit. For example, if a Charging model is in contact with a Wall and rolls to hit towards an opponent with Distracting (1), first apply the -1 from being in contact with a Wall, then apply the -1 from Distracting, unless the model already hits on 5+. • Difficulties (ie., things in the form of X+) can also be modified by addition or subtraction. To work out how a modifier applies to a difficulty of X+ we use the following formula: [difficulty score] – [modifier] = [new difficulty score]. For example, an attack wounding on 4+ with a +1 to-wound modifier, now wounds on 3+. • Always and Never: some rolls always or never succeed or fail on certain results, whereas some Characteristics always or never have a certain value or range of values. • Restrictions: after applying all modifications, certain limits apply to some Characteristics: • Use only whole numbers: round any fractions up. • No Characteristics can be below 0, not even temporarily. Set any value below 0 to 0. • Armour can never be higher than 6, not even temporary. • Discipline and Agility can never be higher than 10, not even temporary. • A Melee Attack always hits on a ‘6’, and always fails on a ‘1’. • Global and Defensive: when a modifier is referencing a specific model part, but influences Global and/or Defensive Characteristics, apply those modifiers only once for the whole model. When multiple modifiers have the same priority step, apply them in the order that results in the lowest value, or the lowest chance of success.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each Broken unit that was not caught is now Shaken and will Flee from the Combat. Move the units one by one in the order chosen by their owner. First, Pivot the unit so that its Rear Facing is parallel with its Facing that was Engaged with the enemy unit it is Fleeing away from, by Pivoting either exactly 0, 90, or 180 degrees. Then, the Broken unit performs a Flee Move straight forward by the previously rolled Flee Distance (see the Psychology chapter for Flee Move rules).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: There are three different Move Manoeuvres. When a unit moves in the Movement Phase, it must select which Move Manoeuvre it will perform: • Advance Move • March Move • Reform Move Remember that since you are allowed to perform any measurements at any time, it is possible to test a Move Manoeuvre, realise it was not a great idea, and then immediately backtrack and perform a different Move Manoeuvre, unless random events or decisions by the opponent have happened that could influence the decision. It is also customary to mark the starting position, so that backtracking can be done accurately. Reform Moves allow units to tactically adjusts their arrangement on the field, granting them the strategic edge to adapt to new challenges during battle. This controlled shift is used to optimise positioning, formation and facing, white staying mostly in the same spot. Advance Moves provide units with the freedom to manoeuvre on the battlefield, making it a versatile choice for repositioning when preparing to engage with the enemy. March Moves are the fastest but least flexible movement option available to units. It allows them to move quickly in a forward direction. Mid-Move Actions If, for any reasons, the unit’s or an individual model’s position is relevant in the middle of an ongoing Move Manoeuvre (such as when performing a Sweeping Attack or taking a Dangerous Terrain Test), the position of the unit is considered as follow: • The unit must be placed in a viable formation adhering to the Unit Spacing rule (0,5") at the point where it becomes relevant, before continuing the move. If it cannot be placed, the move cannot be performed. Note: During a Snaking Forward Move you still only consider the Front Facing of the moving unit. Each model in a file being represented by the Front Facing of the first model in the file. • When measuring the distance each model moves during a Reform Move, measure from its starting position, to the position it is placed mid-move, and then to its final position. Panic During Moves If a unit has to take a Panic Test during any kind of move, do not take this test until the end of the move. Valid Final Position For the final position of the unit to be considered valid, regardless of which Move Manoeuvre was performed, the following condition must be met. If not, the Move Manoeuvre cannot be performed. • Each corner of the unit’s end position must be within twice its Mobility value (2×Mob inches) of at least one corner’s starting position. Note that this does not mean that each corner must be within 2×Mob inches of its own starting position. For simplicity, measure the corner that is furthest away from the starting position, and check by measuring its distance to the starting position of the closest corner. When reaching the end position, make sure that the corner that travelled furthest is still within 2×Mob of at least one of the corners of the unit’s starting position (marked in red dashed lines in the figure).

characteristics.$text: To leave a unit, move the Attachable Model out of the unit using a Move Manoeuvre. Attachable Models ignore the Unit Spacing rule with regards to the unit they are leaving. The unit that is left behind is not considered to have moved, and is free to perform its own move later in the Phase.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The attack may not be used if the attacking model has made an Advance Move, March Move or Random Move during the current Player Turn.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Move each unit that declared a Pursuit one by one in the order chosen by their owner. First, Pivot the unit so that it is Facing the same direction as the Broken unit it is Pursuing. Then, move the unit straight forward by a distance equal to the previously rolled Pursue Distance. A unit that is performing an Overrun always moves straight forward without Pivoting. If there are Pursuing units on both sides, the Active Player moves all their units first, then the Reactive Player moves their units. If the Pursue Move would bring the Pursuing unit in contact with an obstacle, such as an enemy unit, the Battlefield Edge or an Obstruction, specific rules apply. (For details, see Pursue Moves in the Reference Handbook). * During a Pursue Move, the following objects are considered to be Obstructions: • Impassable Terrain Feature • Friendly units that were not part of the same Combat • Enemy units that Fled from the Combat involving the Pursuing unit

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Positioning your forces well is the cornerstone of effective military strategy. The Movement Phase is a crucial opportunity to redeploy each of your units to the place where it can do the most good, setting up your attacks, bombardments, feints and cunning ploys to pay off in subsequent phases and turns. Troops in military formation must learn a range of orderly manoeuvres to accomplish such movements as efficiently as possible. In the Movement Phase, you can move your units one by one in any order. Choose a unit and perform a Move Manoeuvre. Repeat this for all your eligible and willing units. There are certain restrictions on which units can be moved during the Movement Phase. The following units are not allowed to move: • Units that attempted to Charge in the current Player Turn. • Units that are Engaged in Combat. • Units that are Shaken. • Units that have arrived on the Battlefield using Ambush during the current Player Turn.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Combined Units are moved as a group, following the normal rules for moving units. An Attachable Model can move within its unit’s formation by swapping places with other models, as long as the resulting position is still a valid one (generally in the Front rank). This can be done as part of the following moves: • Move Manoeuvres (Advance, March, and Reform Moves) • Pivots, including Post-combat Pivots and Post-Rally Pivots. Note: this does not include Pivots occurring as part of a Flee or Pursue Move (including Overruns). • Combat Reforms Remember that additional restrictions apply to which positions are valid – see the Melee Phase chapter. Attachable Models are not allowed to move within their unit’s formation under any other circumstances, such as when Charging, Aligning, Pursuing or performing a Flee Move.

characteristics.$text: Health Point losses caused by the attack are multiplied into the value given in brackets (X). If the value is a dice, roll one dice for each unsaved wound from an attack with Multiple Wounds. The number of Health Point losses that the attack is multiplied into can never be higher than the Health Points Characteristic of the target (excluding Health Points lost previously in the battle). For example, if an attack with Multiple Wounds (D6) wounds a unit of Trolls (HP 3) and rolls a ‘5’ for the multiplier, the number of Health Points lost is reduced to 3, even if the Troll unit has already lost one or two Health Points previously in battle.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Panic test is a type of Courage Test taken in certain situations, such as: • A friendly Shaken unit performs a Flee Move through the unit. • • Take the test after completing the Flee Move. • The unit suffered enough Health Point losses in a single phase from Ranged Attacks originating from enemy models to fulfil both the following criteria: • The unit suffered at least 3 Health Points losses, and • The unit suffered an amount of Health Points losses at least equal to 25% of the number of HP the unit had at the start of the Phase. Take the Panic Test immediately after possible casualties have been removed. Ignore Health Point losses suffered while Engaged in Combat. • An enemy unit containing Terror declares a Charge against the unit in the Charge Phase. Units do not take Panic Tests if: • They are Engaged in Combat, or • They are already Shaken, or • They already passed a Panic Test during the same phase. If a unit fails a Panic test, it immediately becomes Shaken. Note: this does not mean that the unit performs a Flee Move.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Against Close Combat Attacks, the model gains one of the following effects, whichever would result in a higher Defensive Skill: • The model gains +1 Defensive Skill. • The model’s Defensive Skill is always set to the Offensive Skill of the attacker. Parry cannot be used against models that use Dual-Wield.

characteristics.$text: Now units entirely with Vanguard can make their Vanguard Move. First, the Defender selects one of their Deployed units containing no Characters: that unit gains Vanguard (3"), and must be the first unit to perform a Vanguard Move. (Note: a unit that already has Vanguard can still be selected: the effects are just not cumulative. If no such unit can be selected, the Defender may select any unit with Vanguard to perform the first Vanguard Move). Then, the players alternate moving their units entierly with Vanguard one by one, until all units that can and want to make a Vanguard Move have done so. Remember that per the Vanguard rule, no model can move further than 12", or end within 6" of an enemy unit. See Model Rules for further details.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When performing a Pivot, first mark the Centre of the unit. Then temporarily remove the unit from the Battlefield, and place it back facing any direction, while keeping its Centre in the same position as before. Models may be repositioned within the unit, as long as the number of files does not change. No single model can be moved further than twice its Mobility (see Characteristic Profiles in the Definitions and Terminology chapter) from its starting to its ending position. Check by measuring the direct path of the centre of each model’s base.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Unless stated otherwise, Attachable Models must be placed in the front rank of the unit they are joined to. If this is not possible (e.g. due to the Front rank already being filled with other Attachable Models), they must instead be placed as far forward as possible in the unit.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: If the attack hits with a natural to-hit roll of ‘6’, it automatically wounds with no roll to wound needed. Shooting Attacks using Hopeless Shots wound automatically only if the first to-hit roll is a natural ‘6’. Note that the second to-hit roll must still be successful in order to hit the target. If the attack can be turned into more than one hit (e.g. a hit with Battle Focus), only a single hit, chosen by the attacker, automatically wounds. All other hits must roll to wound as normal.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Any unit that was Engaged during this Round of Combat, but no longer is, and that did not perform a Pursue Move, can now perform a Post-Combat Pivot using the rules for a Pivot Manoeuvre. (see the Movement Phase chapter.) A unit that performs a Post-Combat Pivot, whatever its reason, cannot Declare any Charges in the Charge Phase of the next Player Turn. (If the next Player Turn is your opponent’s, the unit can Declare Charges as normal in your next Player Turn).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Potions and Scrolls are Magic Items that provide temporary effects when consumed by a model. The following rules apply to all Potions and Scrolls, unless specifically mentioned otherwise: • Potions and Scrolls can be activated at the start of any phase, or during Choosing Equipment and Abilities in a Round of Combat. • Their effects (including Characteristic modifiers and Attack Attributes) are only applied to the model part taking the Magic Item, and do not affect other model parts such as mounts.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: An attack with Press of Ranks gains +1 to wound, to a maximum of 3+.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Behold, a rare and unique quality. Units, attacks and spells can have key words called Properties attached to them. Properties describe the unit’s origin, allegiance, elemental effects, equipment, or other defining attributes. Properties can always be identified by their names being displayed in grey and italics. Properties are rules that do not possess any innate or direct effects. Instead, Properties are only used as triggers for other rules. For example, a rule might restrict Characters from joining a unit unless it possesses the right Clan Property.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: When rolling to wound with a Psychic Attack, replace the target’s Resilience with its Discipline.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Every commander must face the reality that their troops might not always obey their orders. Soldiers who lack proper military training and discipline may not be able to execute more complex field operations satisfactorily. And when you ask even the hardiest warrior to face monstrous terrors, or stand firm when their comrades perish and flee, you should be prepared for the eventuality that their resolve may falter. In The 9th Age: Skirmish Campaigns, there are two types of Psychology Tests that represent a warrior’s mental state and ability to follow orders: Command and Courage. When a unit must perform a Command or Courage Test, roll 2D6 and compare the result with the unit’s Discipline (see Characteristic Profiles in the Definitions and Terminology chapter). If the result is equal to or lower than the Discipline value, the test is passed. Otherwise, it is failed.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Units may suffer from various psychological states, which can limit their actions. It is recommended to use markers to indicate the current state of each unit. Note that units can be in multiple states simultaneously.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Before moving any unit, check: • Which Pursuing unit would be led to a Charge due to its Pursue Move, ignoring other Pursuing units. • Which Arc the centre of the Pursuing unit’s Front Facing is located in, For each enemy unit that might be Charged as part of the Pursue Move: if the Pursue Move will lead to a Charge, it will be in the Facing determined at this point. The Charging units will be moved first. The order must be chosen, so that the number of units that successfully completes a Charge is as high as possible. The remaining Pursuing units will be moved afterwards, in an order chosen by their owner. 1. Pivot The Pursuing unit Pivots so that it is Facing the same direction as the pursued unit or, if that unit was removed as a casualty, the direction the pursued unit would have had, if not removed as a casualty. Ignore the Unit Spacing rule during this Pivot. After the Pivot, one of the four situations will arise. If more than one is applicable, only apply the uppermost one: • Enemy unit: if, after the Pivot, the Front Facing of the Pursuing unit would be in contact with the Unit Boundary of an enemy unit that did not Flee from the same Combat, it Declares a Charge towards that unit, which cannot perform any Charge Reactions. (If there is more than one possible target, the Pivoting unit chooses which unit to Charge.) To perform the Charge Move, remove the Pursuing unit from the Battlefield, then place it back following the rules below: • It cannot change formation. • Its Front Facing must be in contact with the enemy unit’s Target Facing (determined before the Pivot). • The centre of the Pursuing unit must move as short a distance as possible from its position before the Pivot, while still allowing a valid position following the Unit Spacing Rule after the Initial Align Move. Afterwards, perform the Initial Align Move (see the Charge Phase chapter; in case of an Unaligned Charge, only perform the Initial Align Move, not the Special Align Move). If there is not enough room to place the Pursuing unit in contact, treat the enemy unit as an Obstruction instead. • Battlefield Edge: if, after the Pivot, the Front Facing of the Pursuing unit would be in contact with (or outside) the Battlefield Edge, the unit instead performs a Post-Combat Pivot, and then moves no further (i.e. ignore step 2.: Forward Ahead). If it is not possible to perform this Post-Combat Pivot in a way that puts the unit in a valid end position, treat the Battlefield Edge as an Obstruction instead. • Obstruction: if, after the Pivot, the Front Facing of the Pursuing unit would be in contact with an Obstruction, the unit instead Pivots so that it faces a direction as close as possible towards the same direction that the Pursued unit is Facing (or would be Facing, if it was removed as a casualty), while following the Unit Spacing rule. The unit then moves no further. • Free to move: if, after the Pivot, the Front Facing of the Pursuing unit is not in contact with any other unit, Battlefield Edge nor Obstruction, proceed to step 2: Forward Ahead. 2. Forward Ahead Without moving the Pursuing unit, check what the first Obstacle, would be, within the rectangle formed by extending its Front Facing directly ahead of the unit a distance equal to the rolled Pursue Distance. If more than one of these situations is applicable, apply only the uppermost one. The Unit Spacing rule is ignored when doing this check and for all movement during Forward Ahead. • Enemy unit: if the first Obstacle would be the Unit Boundary of an enemy unit that did not Flee from the same Combat, the Pursuing unit Declares a Charge towards that unit, using its Pursue Distance roll as its Charge Range. If there is more than one possible target, the Pursuing unit chooses which one to Charge. The charged unit may not perform any Charge Reactions. The Pursuing unit immediately performs a Charge Move towards the previously determined Target Facing, following all the normal Charge Move rules including: Align Moves, Unaligned Charge and Blocked Path if applicable. If the Charge cannot be completed, the unit does not perform a Failed Charge Move, but treats the enemy unit as an Obstruction instead. If the Pursuing unit joins a Combat that has already been fought or was created during this Melee Phase, it will be resolved in the next Melee Phase, with the Charging unit still counting as Charging. If the Pursuing unit instead joins a Combat that was not created and has not been fought yet during the same Melee Phase, it will then fight again and can Pursue again this Phase. • Battlefield Edge: if the first Obstacle would be the Battlefield Edge, move the unit straight forward until it touches the Battlefield Edge, then immediately perform a Post-Combat Pivot. • Obstruction: if the first Obstacle would be an Obstruction, move the unit straight forward until just before it enters into contact with the Obstruction. • Free to move: if the Front Facing of the Pursuing unit would not come in contact with any Obstacle, move it straight forward by its Pursue Distance. 3. Valid Position? At the end of the Pursue Move, check if the unit is in a valid position following the Unit Spacing rule. It cannot be in contact with any enemy unit it did not Declare a Charge towards, but can be within 0.5" of Impassable Terrain or other units (such as friendly units that were part of the same Combat). If the unit is not in a valid position, at the end of the move, backtrack it to its last valid position where it follows the Unit Spacing rule. Example of two units Pursuing into the same enemy unit.a) Unit D loses the Combat, Breaks, and Flees 7". The owner of the winning units chooses to roll for unit A’s Pursue Distance first: 6", which is not enough to catch the Fleeing unit. Unit B’s Pursue Distance is 7", which is equal to or higher than unit D’s Flee Distance: the Fleeing unit is immediately removed as a casualty. Unit C’s Pursue Distance is 5". b) When checking which units will Charge an enemy unit during their Pursuit, before moving any Pursuing unit, it turns out that both unit A and unit B will Charge unit E: both units thus declare a Charge against unit E. Unit C will not Charge any enemy units. c) Now units A and B perform their Pursue Moves first. During this move, they can move through one another ignoring the Unit Spacing rule. Otherwise, they move using the normal rules for Charge Moves (ie. one Wheel allowed, Maximising Contact, etc.). In order to maximise the number of models and units in contact, unit A aligns its Front Facing with unit E’s, while unit B moves into corner to corner contact with unit E. Afterwards, unit C Pivots and moves its Pursue Distance straight forward.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: The attack does not suffer the -1 to-hit modifier for Moving and Shooting.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: Whenever the model loses a Health Point, it gains +1 Att. Whenever it Recovers or Raises a Health Point, it suffers -1 Att

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Raising Health Points is similar to Recovering, with the exception that it can bring back models that have been removed as casualties. When Raising Health Points, lost Health Points on models in the unit (excluding Attachable Models) are first Recovered, followed by bringing back models. Each raised model must fully recovered all its Health Points before another model can be raised. The total number of models in the unit cannot exceed its starting number; any excess raised Health Points are lost. Raised models are placed in the Rear Rank if it is incomplete, or form a new Rear Rank if the current one is complete. In units with only one rank, a raised model can either be placed in the Front Rank, or the player can declare the Front Rank complete and create a new rank behind it (remember that a unit cannot voluntarily have more ranks than files, unless it is wide enough to have a Proper Rank). Any model that cannot be placed in a valid position, following the Unit Spacing rule, is lost. Any used One use only effects or destroyed equipment are not regained. Raised models are subject to the same ongoing effects as their unit.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The Battle of Merton’s Pass, AS 77, was fought between the dwarves of Nevaz Derom and the last survivors of the warherd originally led by Bragh, the Black Bull, who had been slain by Sunna. The dwarven exploratory force was scattered by a sudden rush of hidden beasts, defending their valley refuge. But having fled in all directions, the dwarves rediscovered their courage – one imagines a certain amount of mumbled embarrassment – and the celebrating beasts soon found themselves trapped between armed companies on every side. They say you can still hear the mournful lowing in Mertons Pass on cold nights. It’s a classic study in military history, though I’d advise you to skip Cagilio’s overlong treatise on dwarven tactics.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: During the Rally Phase, the Active Player’s Shaken units must take a Command Test, called a Rally Test. Roll tests one by one in any order. Units Engaged in Combat cannot take Rally Tests. • If the Rally Test is passed, the unit stops being Shaken and may immediately make a Pivot (see the Movement Phase chapter). • If the Rally Test is failed, the unit Pivots to face directly away from the centre of the closest non- Shaken enemy unit, and then performs a Flee Move (see the Psychology chapter). Remember that if a unit initiates a Flee Move whilst Decimated, it is removed as a casualty. Remember that if any Decimated unit that performs a Flee Move is removed as casualty.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Some model parts have random values for one or more Characteristics, such as Attack Value D6+1. Roll for the value each time immediately before it is used. In the case of an Offensive Characteristic, the rolled value is used for all simultaneous attacks from that model part. When several model parts in the same unit have a random value for a Characteristic, roll separately for each model part.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Models with this rule are moved during step 2 of the Movement Phase Sequence. Choose one of your models with Random Movement and perform a Random Move. Repeat this process, each time choosing a new model that has not yet moved in the Movement Phase. To perform a Random Move, choose a direction to move the model in. Then roll the dice specified within the brackets of the rule (X). Move the model the resulting distance in inches in a straight line in the direction previously chosen. The following also applies: • If the model comes into contact with an enemy model, the move is halted as soon as it reaches base contact, and the model counts as Charging. No Interception is possible. • Friendly models are passed through. • The model moves freely over Obstacles (terrain pieces up to 1" high). • The model moves freely across gaps up to 1" wide and up and down Walls up to 1" high (vertical height). For this purpose, any Crevice up to 1" tall may be counted as a Wall. • If the Random Move ends within ½" of any model it is extended until the model is clear (unless the Move resulted in a Charge). • If the Random Move takes the model’s centre over an Edge with a drop of 3" or less, it immediately makes a Jump straight down and then continues its Move forwards. Other Edges are treated as Walls (see below). • If the model collides with a Wall, change the direction of the Move as little as possible to continue parallel with the Wall. • The model cannot move normally in the Movement Phase and cannot declare Charges. Whenever it is necessary to know its March Rate, use the potential maximum value of X" as its March Rate. The model cannot perform Magical Moves. • The model loses Swiftstride and can never gain it. • If the model has several instances of Random Movement, use the one with the lowest average (in case of a tie, the owner chooses which one to use).

sharedProfiles.name: Rank-and-File Models in a Combined Unit Wiped Out

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When all the Rank-and-File models in a combined unit are wiped out, but there are still Attachable Models left, they form a smaller combined unit. This smaller unit is treated as the same unit for effects and Panic Tests.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Some spells or abilities allow units and models Recover Health Points lost during the battle. The amount of Health Points that can be Recovered is specified in the ability. Recovering Health Points cannot bring back models that have been removed as casualties, and cannot increase a model’s Health Points above its starting value (any excess Health Points are lost). Attachable Models inside a combined unit cannot Recover Health Points from spells or abilities that allow a unit to Recover Health Points. Such models can only Recover Health Points when it is specified that they may. Sometimes people say to Klepa, hey Klepa, you sold me this iron kettle that sploded first time it boiled. Or Klepa, you promised this magic amulet would fix my toenails and now all I got is nubs for feet. Or Mr Klepa, you’re under arrest for sale of rabid gnasher-dasher disguised as fluffy pet gerbil. And I say, I told you – Klepa products always work. Just sometimes they work too much. That’s traditional goblin method, you can’t per-see-coot me for my culture! So yes, when we see foolish wizards whose spells work too much, we admire that enthusiasticity. Better to go big and learn something exciting than to be tame, boring, careful, sucks-ex-full all your life, that’s common sense. Wizards don’t mind too much about common sense, seems like. Magic comes at a cost, they say – like Klepa merch and dice. ’Cept Klepa costs are lowest this side of Wasteland, but magic costs very high. Cast a spell wrong, it’ll turn you into a pile of cinders, or suck your soul out your nostrils. That’s what I call steep!

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: To do a Reform Move, pick the unit up from the battlefield and put it back with the following restrictions: • The Centre of the unit cannot travel further than half the unit’s Mobility (in inches). • The formation of the unit may change, but the number of Files cannot change by more than 1 . Note: Generally no unit can voluntarily have more ranks than files, see Models and Units in the Definitions and Terminology chapter). • Each model is considered to have moved from its starting position to its end position, around Obstructions where needed; no single model can move further than twice its Mobility. When measuring each model’s move, it is considered to move independently of its unit. While moving: • Models are treated as their own unit following the Unit Spacing rule. • Can ignore other models from the same unit, but not from other units. • Cannot move further than twice its Mobility (in inches). To move a model you: • Pivot the model • Perform a Snaking Forward Move Repeat steps 1 and 2 in any combination and as many times as needed. At the end of this move, all models come back together again into a viable formation, as described above. Then check for Valid Final Position. ReferenceManualColorSimplified Reform Move In practice, for the vast majority of Reform and Advance Moves, there is no need to consider the movements of individual models. The upper image shows the technical way to perform a Reform Move: moving models one by one (grey dotted lines), and measuring distance the centre of each model moved (black dotted line). The lower image show a simplified method to perform a Reform Move: move the unit as a whole, potentially readjusting formation by adding or removing files. Measure the distance moved by the Centre of the unit, while making sure that no single model moves further than twice its Mobility (this can typically be checked by measuring the distance travelled by the models that have moved the furthest). ReferenceManualColorExample of Reform Move

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: During the Injury Phase, before making a roll on an Injury Table with a model with Regeneration, roll a D6. On a result of X+ the following roll on the Injury Table is automatically treated as a Full Recovery result.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Remove all models in Engaged units that are Shaken as casualties. Remember that units Engaged in Combat do not take Panic Tests. Therefore, the most common way for a Shaken unit to find itself in Combat, is if it gets charged when it was already Shaken.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Multiple attempts at casting a Replicable spell can be made in the same Magic Phase without suffering the normal -3 modifier to the Casting Roll (or -1 in the case of Bound Spells). Note that the spell still can not be attempted multiple times to be cast by the same Wizard.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Attacks allocated against the model’s Health Pool must reroll successful to-wound rolls. If Resistance is associated with an Attack Attribute, Property or Rule in brackets (X), then it only applies against attacks with that Attack Attribute or made by a model with that Property or Rule.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Resolve Melee Attacks from models in the Combat, in descending Agility Order. For each attack, follow the Attack Sequence as defined in the Attacks chapter. This includes models from both sides involved in the Combat.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: After determining Deployment Type and Victory Conditions, both players roll a D6 (a usual 6-sided dice, see Dice in the Definitions and Terminology chapter), rolling again until one player rolls higher. The player who rolls the highest, decides which player will be the Defender; the other player will be the Attacker.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Ruins can be represented for example by rubble, abandoned farmsteads or ancient sites of symbolic or arcane power. Ruins have the following rules: Covering Terrain (Hard Cover, Height 3) for units in contact.# Dangerous Terrain (6+).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Illustrated Rulebook The Illustrated Rulebook contains a streamlined version of the main rules needed for playing the game, alongside art, miniature images and lore. Appendices Appendices are an integral component of the core rules, and are used in most games. There are two appendices to the Illustrated Rulebook: • Illustrated Rulebook – Appendix I: Model Rules -- Additional and unique rules that specific models possess. • Illustrated Rulebook – Appendix II: Arcane Compendium -- The compendium contains spells from the ten different Paths of Magic, along with the common Magic Items and special Leadership Skills. Season Pack This document includes additional Deployment Types, maps, Primary and Secondary Objectives, catering towards more advanced games. Reference Handbook This handbook includes all rules from the Illustrated Rulebook, plus Appendix I: Model Rules and Appendix II: Arcane Compendium documents. Additionally, it includes extended rules text to cover for intricate and complex battlefield situations. We recommend that players who prefer to understand complex situations in advance and fully grasp the nuances of all rule interactions turn directly to this document. For new players and those who prefer to deal with intricate scenarios as they arise, we suggest starting with the Illustrated Rulebook and only consulting the Reference Handbook when specific situations occur that are not fully covered in the Illustrated Rulebook. This document is the Illustrated Rulebook, containing a streamlined version of the main rules needed for playing the game alongside art, miniature images and lore. In addition to this, you will need a few more documents to play a full game of T9A. Army Books The rules for the different armies are found in Army Books. Within these, you will find army composition rules, unit and model rules, characteristics, and so on. Supplements Supplements are optional add-ons to the game that require an agreement with the opponent before using. It is the tenth century of the Ninth Age. An Age of Peace, they say. An Age of Respite. An Age of Exploration and Rebuilding, following the many Ages of Ruin and the great Inferno. And yet everywhere, the shadow of war looms. The peoples of the world have rebuilt, indeed: perhaps too far, with too much ambition. They must contend with elder powers of elves and dwarves who have regained their former glory. With so-called barbarian tribes of ogres, orcs, goblins and beasts herds, who display a strength and hunger for battle like never before. With ancient necromantic dynasties reawoken, with renewed cabals of scheming Night Lords, with the devotees of Dark Gods flocking in ever-greater numbers, ushering otherworldly servants from beyond the Veil. With strange species of reptiles and rodents, long thought extinct, threatening a return to ancient empires of enslavement. And finally, they must contend with humanity itself, which has perhaps grown the most of all. Since the coming of the legendary hero Sunna, it has developed from primitive tribes into mighty nations whose will to conquer knows no bounds. It is an Age of Promise. An Age of Possibility. An age where everything is to play for. Where any of the world’s powers could soon become master of all others. Where the world itself holds its breath. No longer an Age of Peace: it has become an Age of Battle.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: In order to keep rules clear and tidy, the following text formatting is used: Text in a grey box denotes designer notes. In these are the designers giving some insights into intent behind rules, alternate ways to play the game, or shortcuts to speed things up. • CAPITALIZATION is used for words/phrases that are defined in this book, such as Round of Combat, unless they are common words with no elaborate game definition like model or unit, but Combat is since it is not used like the common British term. • Bold font or text is used to highlight specific words. It is also used in Army Books to emphasise Model Rules specified in the same unit entry. • Italic font marks reminders, examples, clarifications, and other content that are not direct rules. • Grey-coloured text is used for figure and table captions, item restrictions, repetitive content, and Properties, which is a special type of keyword that doesn’t transfer any direct rules. • Hyperlinks can be found in the electronic version of this document, and the page footer includes hyperlinks to key sections. • Pink text is unique to the Reference Handbook . This Handbook covers corner-cases and specific circumstances that are not expected to be relevant in the majority of games. The Handbook is a copy of the Illustrated Rulebook with additional sections added to cover these corner-cases.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When wounds are inflicted on a unit, there are two types of saves that the defender can make to potentially negate the damage: Armour Saves and Special Saves. When taking saves, the owner of the attacked model rolls a D6 and compares it with the needed score to pass the save. See the details below for how to pass Armour Saves and Special Saves. If successful, the wound is ignored. First roll Armour Save, and then, if this is not passed, roll the Special Save (provided the model has one). If the Special Save is failed, or the model does not have a Special Save, a wound is inflicted. Proceed to Losing Health Points and Casualties.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Scoring models are able to interact with objectives and can score you points to win the game. All models that are Infantry or Cavalry are Scoring. A model that is Knocked Down loses Scoring for as long as it is Knocked Down.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Models with this rule may be deployed using Special Deployment rules. All models that will be deployed using the Scout rule must be declared during step 7 of the Pre-Game Sequence (after Determining Deployment Zones), starting with the player that picked the Deployment Zone first. Scout deployment is conducted on step 4 of the Deployment Phase (Deploy Scouting Models). If both players have Scouting models, alternate model placement (one model at a time), starting with the player who first completed their normal deployment. Scouting models have two deployment options: • Fully inside your Deployment Zone, using the normal deployment rules • Anywhere on the Battlefield, at least 12" away from enemy models Scouting models that are placed outside their Deployment Zone may not declare Charges in the first Game Turn.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When a unit fails a Panic Test, a Break Test, or chooses the Flee! Charge Reaction, it becomes Shaken. A Shaken unit is unable to perform voluntary actions. This includes declaring Charges, moving in any way other than a Flee Move, shooting, generating Magic Dice, casting spells, or activating Magic Items that require a voluntary activation. There is one exception: the unit may still choose to Flee! or Hold! as a Charge Reaction. Remember that if unit is Shaken, it temporarily stops being Scoring. This lasts until it is no longer Shaken. A Shaken unit that finds itself Engaged in Combat is removed as casualty at step 1 of the Round of Combat Sequence. In order to remember which units are Shaken, we recommend that Shaken units are clearly marked. This can either be done with specific markers or tokens to indicate a unit is Shaken, or if you do not have such markers, a commonly used method for marking Shaken units is to take one model from the front rank of the Shaken unit, and put it lying face down next to the unit.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: After deciding on the scale of the game and writing their Army Lists, the next step is to share Army Lists and all relevant information about the upcoming game. Sharing Army Lists before the game starts allows both players to look up the rules that apply to the units to be involved in the game, so that they understand how those will function and can plan their strategy accordingly, avoiding any unpleasant surprises, and minimising the time spent reading rules while playing.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The wielder gains +1 Armour. Models on foot fighting with a Shield and a Sword gain Parry. To gain the benefits from a Shield while in combat, the model must dedicate a Hand to it.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Shield Enchantments are upgrades that apply to Shields. An Enchanted Shield follows the rules for both the original Shield and the Shield Enchantment. The following rules apply to all Shield Enchantments, unless specifically mentioned otherwise: • The effect of a Shield Enchantment only applies when the bearer of the Enchanted Shield is Using a Shield (remember that a model part cannot use a Shield to protect against Melee Attacks when it is using a Two-Handed weapon in Combat). • Characteristic modifiers, Model Rules, and all other rules associated with Shield Enchantments follow the same rules as for Armour Enchantments.

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: A model part with Shoot in Extra Rank may use Shooting Attacks from one additional rank. Normally, this means that it will be able to make Shooting Attacks from the third rank.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: There are many kinds of shooting used by the armies of the 9th Age, from bows, guns and thrown weapons to arcane devices and grand artillery machines. With the exception of magical spells, the Shooting Phase is your chance to unleash all of your ranged attacks at the foe, thinning their forces without the risks of close melee. But of course the enemy may not make it easy, taking cover behind any battlefield shelter they can find to foil your attempts at a clear shot. The Shooting Phase consists of the following steps: 1 & Choose one of your units and perform a Shooting Attack with it. 2 & Select the target of the attack and which models in the unit will shoot. Each model must have Line of Sight to at least one model in the Target unit and be within its effective range. 3 & Resolve the Shooting Attack. 4 & Repeat steps 1 to 3 with a different unit that has not yet performed a Shooting Attack during this phase, if desired. When all units that can and want to shoot have done so, the Shooting Phase ends.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Once the models that will shoot are established, they each make as many shots as indicated in their weapon’s profile. Roll to hit by rolling a D6 for each shot and compare its result to the weapon’s Aim (written in brackets after the weapon’s name). For example, a dwarf warrior has Throwing Weapons (5) with Shots 2. When this model shoots, roll two D6: each roll of 5+ is a successful hit. For each hit, follow the Attack Sequence to determine the damage (see the Attacks chapter). Everyone loves a good stab. But sometimes stabbing people can be more hassle than it’s worth. You have to get up close, so there’s the unlovely risk of being stabbed right back. That’s why lots of people prefer shooting – what we goblins call stabbing from a distance. Beautiful to see, really: all the ways people have invented for battling far off, nice and impersonal. Arrows are an easy one, but nowadays there’s guns too, all kinds. And big machines with springs for lobbing your classic rock, or spurting out fire, or sending off spells… Speaking of spurting fire, some things don’t even need a machine. Dragons is a scary one. Thought they were miffy-logical til one showed up in Avras, bold as brass. Weird creatures, dragons. Love to collect stuff, but won’t haggle with merchants. Won’t let anyone near them except one special friend they call a rider. You almost never see two dragons together, but some say they have big secret meetings where no one can see. Don’t bear thinking about – defnitly wouldn’t want to try stabbing one of them!

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The Active Player gains additional Magic Dice from the following sources: • One free additional Magic Dice. • Magic Dice from models with Channel. • Magic Dice stored from the previous phase (see Storing Magic). Note: each non- Shaken model with Channel (X) adds X Magic Dice. The most common source of Channel are Wizards: • Wizard Adepts have Channel (1). • Wizard Masters have Channel (2). • Wizard Conclaves have Channel (1), unless it is a Wizard Conclave (1). -1 I hope you haven’t been listening to any criminal goblins. That would be almost as inadvisable as talking to an undergraduate! Herr Sigmund Selig here, Professor Emeritus; you may call me The Sage. Forgive my tardiness, but I’d just seen a paper by that buffoon of a provost from Eichtal, claiming that the Flux responds to the seniority of the mage who calls upon it. Naturally I had to write a treatise in response – the Flux is simply the vulgar term for the flow of magic into and around our Realm, and all proper experiments demonstrate that though a wizard might draw more of this substance to themselves by “channelling”, they cannot increase the total magical resources in the vicinity, which is entirely random. Thank goodness I was in time to correct you on that!

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Units containing Skirmisher adopt a unique formation, called a Skirmish Formation. Instead of being in contact with each other, these models are placed 12.5mm apart from each other (roughly half an inch, see the figure below). These gaps between the models are considered part of the unit for Cover and Line of Sight purposes, and have the same Height as the unit. Other than this gap between models, units with Skirmisher follow the normal rules for forming units and therefore have a Front, two Flanks, and a Rear Facing, can perform Supporting Attacks, and so on. Units in Skirmish Formation can only be joined by Attachable Models that have the same Height as the unit. Unless an Attachable Model has the exact same base size as all Rank-and-File models in the unit, it is considered Mismatched for the purpose of placement within the unit. The unit ceases to be in Skirmish Formation when all models with Skirmisher have been removed. When this happens, contract their Skirmish Formation into a normal formation when returning the unit into a valid formation, without moving the centre of the first rank. If Engaged in Combat, nudge any unit as normal to maintain contact. See figure figure/skirmisher for an illustration of this rule. Skirmish formation.An example of a unit in Skirmish Formation with a joined Mismatching Character. All models are 12.5 mm away from each other. The same unit Engaged in Combat. Only darkened models may attack. Models with a dashed frame can attack a Character (either C1 or C2). Models with a lighter shade cannot attack at all.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Snaking Forward Move is broken down into three optional actions, which are carried out in this order: 1 & Initial Forward Move: the unit moves straight forward. 2 & Wheel: the unit is rotated forward around one of its front corners, up to 90 degrees. 3 & Concluding Forward Move: the unit moves straight forward. Most Snaking Forward Moves have a limit to the distance the unit can move. To determine the distance moved, add the distance used for each action to a total: • For Forward Moves (steps 1 and 3), the moved distance is the distance the unit moves forward. • The distance used for the Wheel (step 2) is the distance the outer front corner is moving in the unit’s straight forward direction (see Figure 3). This total cannot exceed the maximum Snaking Forward Move distance, determined by the Move Manoeuvre performed. At the start of every Snaking Forward Move, before moving the unit at all, the unit is collapsed into a line - its Front Facing. Every part of the unit behind this line moves straight forward until they meet the Front Facing. The unit then moves forward as this single line. Note that the models still have a width (but no depth), equal to the width of their base; and that this move can cause Dangerous Terrain Tests, if used during a move type that triggers Dangerous Terrain Tests, such as a Charge or March Moves. When the unit reaches its final position at the end of all Snaking Forward Moves, it expands to regain its depth again. This is done by having the rear parts of the unit move straight back from the Front Facing, until they reach their original position within the unit formation and/or a Viable Formation is achieved.Most Snaking Forward Moves have a limit to the distance the unit can move. Add the distance used for each action to a total. This total cannot exceed the maximum Snaking Forward Move distance. For Forward Moves (steps 1 and 3), the moved distance is the distance the unit moves forward. The distance used for the Wheel (step 2) is the distance the outer front corner is moving in the unit’s straight forward direction (see Figure figure/snakingForward). Only consider the unit’s Front Facing during the entire Manoeuvre (e.g. for the Unit Spacing rule) until after the Manoeuvre is completed, where the whole Unit Boundary is again taken into account (i.e. the unit must abide by the Unit Spacing rule at its final position). If the Snaking Forward Move is made as part of a Charge Move, the Manoeuvre also includes the Initial Align Move (i.e. only consider the Front Facing until after the Initial Align Move has been completed). Snaking Forward Move Simplified Snaking Forward Move blank line When executing a Snaking Forward Move, you can quickly check possible moves by using a measuring stick that has the same length as the width of the unit. Place this stick parallel with the unit’s Front Facing, then move the stick using the Snaking Forward Move rules. This stick represents the Front Facing of the unit. • If you are not happy with the end position, put this stick back along the Front Facing of the unit and try again. • Once you are happy with the position, leave the stick in its place and now move the unit to this position, aligning its Front Facing with the measuring stick. During this rotation, the unit is removed from the table, and then placed back facing a new direction. When measuring a Pivot, it’s recommended that you start off by marking the Centre of the unit. You can do this without moving the unit, by placing four markers around it, such that they form a cross with its centre under the unit’s Centre. Then remove the unit and place it back, with its Centre again on the centre of the marked cross. B. Example of a Wheel. The unit is rotated forward, around one of its front corners. The distance the unit is considered to have travelled is equal to the distance the unit’s outer front corner has moved in the straight forward direction, indicated by the red line in the figure. The example Wheel moved 4". When measuring a Wheel, it is recommended to place a measuring stick next to the unit and aligned towards the unit’s forward direction. Then wheel the unit to the wanted position, and then read off the distance from the measuring stick by checking how far the front corner moved, as indicated by the dotted line in the figure above.
