characteristics.$text: If a wound is not saved by the Armour Save, the defender may negate the attack, even an Unmodifiable one, with its Special Save, if it has one. Special Saves work like Armour Saves, except they are unaffected by Armour Penetration. A natural roll of ‘1’ or ‘2’ is always a failure. There are two types of Special Saves: Aegis and Regeneration, each explained in detail in the Model Rules section. A model is only allowed to roll one Special Save roll for each attack.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Models that can cast spells of any kind are Casters. Casters able to cast Learned Spells are also Wizards. If a Caster has a choice between spells, or knows any Learned Spells, the chosen spells must be written on the Army List. Casters know different numbers of spells, and select them as described in their unit entries, except for Wizards, who all follow the same general rules for selecting their Learned Spells: Each of the following Wizard types must choose a Path of Magic to select spells from. Which Paths it has access to is specified under each Wizard’s unit entry. The chosen Path of Magic must be written on the Army List. Wizards know and select a different number of Learned Spells depending on their type: • Wizard Apprentice: 1 spell, that is the Apprentice Spell (#1). • Wizard Adept: 3 spells chosen from Apprentice Spell and Adept Spells (#1 – #4). • Wizard Master: 5 spells chosen from Apprentice Spell, Adept Spells, and Master Spells (#1 – #6). The only kind of Wizard that does not select a Path is a Wizard Conclave (X). It instead select spells from the list specified in its Unit Entry. If it is either of the following types, then the Wizard does not select a Path of Magic: • Wizard Conclave (X): X spells from the list of Learned Spells specified under its unit entry. • Protean Magic (X): X Apprentice Spells, chosen from any Path of Magic it has access to. During Pre-game Selections, Casters may Swap Spells. For details, see 3.2 Pre-game Selections. To save time and space on Army List writing, we recommend that the Wizard level of a model is followed by the Path name with the numbers of the selected spells in brackets. For example, Wizard Adept, Alchemy (2, 3, 4).

characteristics.$text: A model part with Stand and Shoot may perform an out of sequence Shooting Attack, when an enemy unit successfully performs a Charge Move that brings it in contact with the model part’s unit, if the following conditions are met: • The model part’s unit is not Engaged in Combat with any other units. Note: this means that during a Combined Charge, only the first Charging Unit moved can be targeted, except if the Charging Unit is removed at the end of its move. As long as the Charging Unit is removed at the end of its move, there is no limit on the amount of times a unit can Stand and Shoot. • The enemy unit Charges the model part’s unit in its Front Facing. • The enemy unit started the Charge further away than its Charge Speed (using the lowest Charge Speed in the unit.) • The Charge was not done as part of a Pursue Move. This is a Shooting Attack that does not require Line of Sight, can be done even if the enemy unit is not in the shooter’s Front Arc, and is always resolved against the target unit’s (i.e., the Charging unit’s) Front Facing.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Attachable Models with Stand Behind are not required to have their Front Facing as far forward as possible within their unit this generally means that the model can be positioned anywhere within its unit. characteristics.$text: The model automatically passes Dangerous Terrain Tests taken due to terrain. Sometimes Strider is linked to a specific type of Terrain, stated in brackets. In this case, models with Strider are considered to have this rule only when interacting with such a type of Terrain.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When a unit containing Stubborn loses a Round of Combat, halve the penalty to its Discipline from the Combat Score difference, rounding fractions up (i.e. towards a larger modifier). If the unit is also Steady, the modifier is first set to no smaller than -2 (following the Steady rules), and then halved, rounding up, to -1. If the unit is Unstable, the Health Point losses due to Unstable are halved, rounding fractions up (i.e. towards more Health Point losses).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Summoned units are units that are created during the game. When Summoning a unit, all its models must be Deployed within the specified Range of the ability. If the unit is summoned as a result of a spell with Type: Ground, at least one model must be placed on the targeted point, and all models must be within the spell’s Range. Summoned models must be placed following the Unit Spacing rule. If the whole unit cannot be Deployed, then no model can be Deployed. Once summoned, the newly created unit operates as a normal unit controlled by the side that Summoned it. Summoned units do not award Victory Points to the opponent when they are removed as a casualty.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: All attacks made by the model become Magical Attacks, including Special Attacks. During step 1 of Recovery in the Satus Phase, the model must pass a Discipline Test in order to Recover a Health Point. This test is considered a Recovery Test. In addition, if the model is Knocked Down, it automatically stops being Knocked Down and instead becomes Dazed until the end of the Player Turn.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The model cannot become Knocked Down. During the Status Phase, the model ignores Recovery (i.e. it does not Recover Health Points during that phase).

characteristics.name: Attack Attribute
characteristics.$text: When a model with Sweeping Attack is within 1" of an Unengaged enemy unit during a Move Manoeuvre (even temporarily), the model’s unit may perform a Sweeping Attack against that enemy unit. This can only be used once per friendly Player Turn. Resolve the Sweeping Attack when the Move Manoeuvre is completed. The attack hits automatically, and counts as a Ranged Attack. Each model part in the unit with Sweeping Attack must use it towards the same enemy unit. The attack causes X hits, resolved with the model part’s Strength, Armour Penetration and Attack Attributes, but not Weapons. If values for Strength, Armour Penetration and additional Attack Attributes are defined in the bracket (Y), these are used instead. In this case, the Sweeping Attack is Unmodifiable.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: After Calculating the Final Combat Score, each unit on the side that lost the Round of Combat must take a Break Test, in an order chosen by the player who lost the Round of Combat. A Break Test is a Courage Test with a negative modifier equal to the difference in Combat Scores. For example, if the Combat Score was 6 to 3, the units on the losing side take their Break Tests with a -3 modifier. Note that rules such as Steady, Solid, Bodyguard and Stubborn can have an impact on what the Discipline modifier ends up as. • If the Break Test is passed, the unit remains Engaged in the Combat. • If the Break Test is failed, the unit is Broken, and will now attempt to Flee from the Combat. -1

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When checking Line of Sight from a Shooting model to the target, also simultaneously check which Facing is the Target Facing. This is done by establishing in which Arc of the Target unit the centre of the Front Facing of the Shooting unit’s is located in: the corresponding Facing is referred to as Target Facing (i.e. it is determined in the same way as for Charging).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Each battlefield is unique, with opportunities and challenges presented by the lie of the land. The ability to use both geographical features and man-made structures to your advantage can make all the difference. Some landscapes can be so treacherous that your forces may even perish if they lack sufficient caution.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: A Terrain Feature is a topographical area on the Battlefield that may be a mixture of Dangerous, Opaque, or Covering Terrain and may possess its own set of additional rules. Most Terrain Features follow the corresponding rules: FieldsfieldsFields can be represented in the game for example by meadows of tall grass, or agricultural enclosures. Fields have the following rules: Covering Terrain (Soft Cover, Height 3) for units in contact.# Flammable: units in contact gain Weakness (Flaming Attacks). Forestforest Forests can be represented for example by jungles, brushwoods, or small groves of trees. Forests have the following rules: Covering Terrain (Soft Cover, Height 5).# Dangerous Terrain (6+, Mount).# Disruptive Terrain. HillshillsHills can be represented for example by elevated plateaus or burial mounds. Hills have the following rules: Elevated Position: a model is considered to have an Elevated Position if it is fully on a Hill. For the purposes of determining Cover and for drawing Line of Sight to or from a model with Elevated Position, ignore intervening models that do not have an Elevated Position. # Opaque Terrain. Remember that Line of Sight can still be drawn into and out of the Terrain Feature. Impassable TerrainimpassableterrainImpassable Terrain can be represented for example by monoliths, cliffs, massive boulders, or buildings. Impassable Terrain has the following rules: Dangerous Terrain (4+) for units making Flee Moves through it.# Impassable: models cannot move into or through an Impassable Terrain Feature (except as part of a Flee Move).# Opaque Terrain. WallswallsWalls can be represented for example by stone, wood, or makeshift structures. Walls have the following rules: Covering Terrain (Hard Cover, Height 3) for units in contact.# Dangerous Terrain (6+, Construct).# Fortified Position Attack Attribute: Melee Attacks from Charging models that are in contact with a Wall suffer a -1 to hit penalty. This also applies to Supporting Attacks made by Charging models over models in contact with a Wall, and to attacks across gaps where the model’s virtual extended base would be in contact with a Wall. RuinsruinsRuins can be represented for example by rubble, abandoned farmsteads or ancient sites of symbolic or arcane power. Ruins have the following rules: Covering Terrain (Hard Cover, Height 3) for units in contact.# Dangerous Terrain (6+). Water TerrainwaterterrainWater Terrain can be represented in the game for example by ponds, swamps, or rivers. Water Terrain has the following rules: Dangerous Terrain (6+, Metal Armour).# Disruptive Terrain.# Soaked: units in contact gain Immune (Flaming Attacks).# Unsure Footing: models in contact cannot use Impact Hits, Stomp Attack.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Terrain represents distinct areas on the battlefield that introduce additional rules that affect models within or interacting with it. These areas are typically represented by modelled terrain that are placed on the board. The most common Terrain Features in the game are explained below. In addition, rules for more Terrain Features can be found in the Season Pack.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: When a unit containing Terror declares a Charge in the Charge Phase, the target must take a Panic Test. If the test is failed, the unit must choose Flee! as its Charge Reaction if allowed to do so (e.g. not already Engaged in Combat, etc.). Units containing Terror are themselves immune to the effects of Terror.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: This game is divided into three main sections, performed in order. 1 & Battle Preparations. Before a game, certain preparations are needed. The players need to put together their armies, prepare the battlefield, agree on Victory Conditions and Deploy their armies. 2 & Game Turns. The 9th Age is a turn-based game played over six Game Turns. Each Game Turn consists of two Player Turns. These are made up of a series of Phases: • Charge Phase • Movement Phase • Magic Phase • Shooting Phase • Rally Phase • Melee Phase 3 & After the Game. After both players have played their six Player Turns, it is time to tally up the Victory Points and check who managed to complete the Primary and Secondary Objectives to determine who is the winner of the game. Greeeetings! I am Klepa, one hundred percent honest and reliable merchant goblin. This is my healthful and fine-smelling accomplice – ah – pet! my charming pet: Fleabag. For smallest of prices, and promise not to talk to mean old city guards, we can be your guides here. Klepa will share all his, er, lawfully ack-quee-zis-shined knowledge about the wide world of the Ninth Age! Such a pleasure to meet a new mark – I mean customer! Customer and friend! Welcome Active & Reactive Player The Active Player is the one currently taking their Player Turn, and the Reactive Player is the one whose Player Turn is not currently happening. Before the first Player Turn, the Defender is the Active Player. Friendly and Enemy The terms friendly and enemy are used to distinguish between units, model, spells, and other effects belonging to the same player (friendly) and units, models, spells, and other effects controlled by the opposing player (enemy). Your First Game Is this your first game? Let’s get you started. First, prepare your battlefield: a large flat surface with model terrain on – a pile of books can be a hill, a mug can be a rock, a mouse pad can be a lake, and so on. Then, challenge a friend to a game where you both command your own miniature army. For a trial run without the commitment of time and resources, we offer downloadable paper cutouts on the T9A website (Essence of War). If you are uncertain about which army to choose, a brief overview of the 16 main armies and their primary themes can be found in the Introduction chapter.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Before casting any Occultism spell, the Caster may select a Health Pool in a friendly unit within 18": this unit loses a number of Health Points equal to 9 - the Discipline in its profile, to a minimum of 1. No Health Pool can be selected more than once per Magic Phase. If The Sacrifice was performed, the Range of the spell is increased by +6".

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The Ninth Age is a time of epic clashes and feats of arms, of legends, myths, monsters and magic. After nine long ages of strife, the many peoples and kingdoms of this high fantasy world have acquired highly developed and often spectacular methods of waging war. With so many great and terrible powers throughout the lands, the future is poised and uncertain: Everything could be decided on the outcome of a single battle. For the reader who wishes to delve deeper into the lore of the Ninth Age, you can discover more of the wider setting in each Army Book, as well as our background-focused publications: the-ninth-age.com/the-world. Among the various cultures, countries, and strange dominions of the world, sixteen great factions are pre-eminent. Each of these powers represents a terrifying military force. Each will attempt to dominate the Ninth Age as they are able, and each has connections that can bring it across the globe. As such, there is never any shortage of reasons for conflict and battle between these mighty armies - as your tabletop games can testify. Few individuals have the chance to see more than a fraction of our world, with its astonishing variety of intelligent races and animal species, plants and cities, cults and wars. I have travelled from Avras to the Kingdom of Vanhu. I’ve seen Sunna’s seeds planted in Virentia and the Great Wall of Tsuandan in the far east of Augea. You could not find another who has travelled a greater distance; I have been protected by the auspice of Sunna, and here I record my knowledge on the geography of our world. Vetia is the land of mankind, where nations of men have reigned for years under the protective sight of the Goddess and her church. There, the powerful nation of Sonnstahl guards all mankind against the dangers of the Wasteland, while to the south the merchant cities of Arcalea ply their trade with the whole of the world. There you will also find the White Mountains, impenetrable hold of the Dwarves. To the west lie the twin cities of Destria, the Kingdom of noble Equitaine, and the enchanted, emerald-green forest of Wyscan, the mysterious dwelling of the sylvan elves. Augea, the immense sister of Vetia, separated from one another by the great Wasteland, home to the servants of the Dark Gods. Crossing east of Avras into this land, you will travel through the Barren Mountains, where the Steel Road starts its winding journey. Here is the dwelling of the Dwarves of the east, named Infernal. The Steel Road runs parallel to the Silk Road to the north, with access controlled by the Ogre Khans. It leads from the Blasted Plains through the Sky Mountains, across the northern part of the human region of Sagarikadesha, finishing its rich path in the glorious land of Tsuandan, where the Dragon Emperor rules over men. Set sail south from Bellatorre, and in three nights you will reach the docks of Port Reynaud, Equitaine’s holdfast in Taphria. Should you dare it, you will never forget the nights spent in the Great Desert, for they are terrible and fascinating all at once. There, following the path of the Napaat river, lie the remains of a truly ancient kingdom with its legends of never-dying monstrosities. In the west stand the fortresses and souks of Qassar, full of exotic smells and tales of evil spirits, the djinn. In the west and southeast of the continent lie vast kingdoms of men; the Koghi Empire and Kingdom of Vanhu respectively. Finally in its south, the forests around the Mfumu river are said to hide some of the most ancient secrets of the world. The Great Ocean divides Vetia from the two western continents, Silexia in the north and Virentia in the south. The Ocean itself is the dominion of elves: there the fleets of the two great nations, the Highborn and their dreaded kin, vie for supremacy. Here lies the main motherland of the Highborn Elves, the proud islands of Celeda Ablan, and Silexia where freedom is a commodity to be traded. On the eastern coast of Virentia mankind too, has established colonies: the imperial city of Fredericksberg, and the port of Aguadulce, of Destria. Beyond them, a lush forest of wonderful colors and inconceivable dan- gers hides the secrets of ancient civilizations. Dividing Virentia from Silexia, the Shattered Sea; a rumoured maelstrom of magic and tempests, from which no vessel returns. --From A New Atlas for the Ninth Age, by Johannes Strabo

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The to-hit roll of a Shooting Attack can be modified, affecting the chance of scoring a successful hit. If the modifier brings the needed score to 7+ or beyond, the attack cannot hit, and a roll of ‘1’ is always considered a miss. Apply the following modifiers to the to-hit roll: • Long Range (-1): if the target is more than half the weapon’s maximum Range away from the Shooting model, apply a -1 to-hit modifier. • Accurate: if the Shooting model part or its weapon has Accurate, ignore the modifier for Long Range. • Moving and Shooting (-1): if the Shooting model’s unit has performed a Move Manoeuvre (Advance, March or Reform*) in this Player Turn, apply a -1 to-hit modifier. • Quick to Fire: if the Shooting model part or its weapon has Quick to Fire, it does not suffer the normal -1 to-hit penalty for Moving and Shooting. • *Only model parts with March and Shoot (or using a weapon with that rule) can shoot after having Marched in the same Player Turn. If they do, the -1 to-hit modifier for Moving and Shooting applies. • Unwieldy (-X): if the Shooting model part or its weapon has Unwieldy and has performed a Move Manoeuvre during the same Player Turn, apply an additional -X to-hit modifier. • Cover: the target could benefit from either Soft Cover or Hard Cover: • Soft Cover (-1): if the target benefits from Soft Cover, apply a -1 to-hit modifier. • Hard Cover (-2): if the target benefits from Hard Cover, apply a -2 to-hit modifier. • Hard Target (X): if the Target unit has Hard Target, apply a -X to-hit modifier. *See Model Rules for the full rules.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Once you have hit your target, you must wound it in order to potentially cause harm. To determine if a hit successfully wounds the target, roll a D6 for each hit. The required roll to wound depends on the difference between the attack’s Strength and the defender’s Resilience, as indicated in the table below. characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: If the Charging Unit cannot perform the Initial Align Move so that it is both fully aligned with the enemy, and the initial point of contact* remains in contact (Align Move conditions 1 and 2), the following rules are used instead: The Charge Move and Align Move(s) must be made in such a way that the initial point of contact on the charged unit, before the Initial Align Move, remains in contact after the Initial Align Move, and such that, at the end of both Align Moves, the Charging Unit’s Front Facing does not cross over the projected line running parallel with the Target Facing. Corresponding to the area marked in red in step 1 of Figure figure/example_Charge_move. After making sure that the Charge will be possible without breaking the above condition, the Charging Unit must satisfy the conditions below as best as possible, in decreasing order of priority: • The initial point of contact on the charged unit, before the Initial Align Move, must remain in contact* after the Initial Align Move. Note that the Charging model that initially made contact is not required to remain in contact. • Minimise the angle between the Front Facing of the Charging Unit and the Target Facing. • The number of models in the target unit that are in contact* (taking into account those Fighting Over Gaps) with enemy units must be maximised. • The number of models in the Charging Unit that are in contact* (taking into account those Fighting Over Gaps) with enemy units must be maximised. *Contact here is referring to contact between Unit Boundaries, including Fighting Over Gaps. After performing the Initial Align Move with the Charging Unit, the charged unit performs a Special Align Move. A unit that is Engaged can never perform a Special Align Move. It is picked up and rotated around the point of contact, such that the angle between the Charging Unit’s Front Facing and the Target Facing is minimised, possibly and ideally fully aligning the units with each other. Note: Any units not fully aligned must Combat Reform whenever possible. See Melee Phase chapter for details.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: The Unit Boundaries of any remaining units are unfrozen, and the models within the unit are rearranged to reform a valid formation. See the Reference Handbook; Maintaining a Viable Formation for details. Afterwards, nudge units that are neither Breaking nor Pursuing back in contact with each other where contact was lost. See the Reference Handbook; Nudge units to maintain contact for details. Nudge units to maintain contact After unfreezing Unit Boundaries and rearranging models within the unit to maintain valid formations, any unit that was Engaged in Combat just before this, but lost contact due to updated Unit Boundaries, is nudged back into contact. This does not apply to units that are about to Flee, nor units that are about to Pursue. Move units one at a time, in the order described below, until all units have either attempted to maintain contact and failed, or are back in contact with the enemy. • Move the Active Player’s units first. • Move all units on each side, in the order that allows the most units to remain in Combat. • If different ways of proceeding bring about the same amount of units remaining in Combat, each owner decides in which order their own units will be nudged. Nudge each unit to maintain contact with the unit(s) it was in contact with before updating Unit Boundaries, following the rules below: • If the unit is in contact with an enemy, it is not nudged. • The unit cannot be nudged through units or Impassable Terrain. • The unit cannot be nudged into contact with any new enemy unit, but can end this move within 1" of other units and Impassable Terrain. • The unit must be moved by the minimum distance required to maintain contact. • The unit must be moved in a straight line: either directly forwards, directly backwards, sideways, or in a combination of two of these directions. • The unit cannot change which of its Facings are in contact with enemies. If these rules do not allow the unit to maintain contact, do not move the unit at all. Units that lose contact follow the rules for No More Foes. If, as a result of updating Unit Boundaries, two or more separate groups of opposing units have been created, subgroup will be treated as a separate Combat from now on. No More Foes When a unit is unable to be nudged back into contact with enemies it previously was in contact with (including due to those enemy units no longer being on the Battlefield, e.g. because they have been removed as casualties, during or outside the Round of Combat, such that it finds itself no longer Engaged in Combat. It may perform a Post-Combat Pivot, or if it was Charging, an Overrun.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Normally, units must maintain a distance of more than 1" from Impassable Terrain and other units both friends and enemies. During ongoing moves, the Unit Spacing requirement is lowered to outside 0.5". At the end a move a unit must be outside 1" again. This means that units are allowed to come within 1", but still outside 0.5" of other units and Impassable Terrain during their moves. A unit can still not come into contact, overlap with their bases, or voluntarily end a move within 1" of either Impassable Terrain or other units. The following moves are an exception to this:: Uncontrolled Move: Charge Moves, Failed Charge Moves, Flee Moves, Pursue Moves, Nudge to Maintain Contact, Combat Reform Moves, and when explicitly stated otherwise. During an Uncontrolled Move a unit is allowed to move, and end within 0.5" of other units and Impassable Terrain, but cannot overlap with their bases, unless explicitly stated otherwise, such as it is in Pivot at the beginning of a Pursuit. If a unit ends a move within 1" of one or more units or Impassable Terrain it may remain within 1" including within 0.5" of those units and Impassible Terrain, until it is outside 1" again. Temporarily removing a unit from the battlefield, such as during a Reform or Pivot, does not count as moving outside 1", unless it is further away than 1" when placed back. If a unit is ever forced to end a move in a invalid position, as determined by the type of move, or overlapping with a Unit Boundary or Impassible Terrain, backtrack the unit to its last valid position.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: For Combined Units consisting entirely of Attachable Models, Matching or Mismatching Bases are determined differently since there are no Rank-and-File models. In such a case, the owner of the unit decides, when the unit is first formed, which model’s base to use in place of Rank-and-File models. Models with the same base, or bases that are a multiple of it, are then considered Matching. If the chosen model leaves the unit or is removed as a casualty, a new model must be chosen as reference for Matching/Mismatching Bases. If possible, this choice must be made so that as few models as possible change their status regarding Matching or Mismatching (normally this means choosing a model with the same base as the model that left the unit).

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Whenever a unit entirely with Unstable would take a Break Test, it suffers instead a number of Health Point losses equal to the amount by which the Combat was lost (with no saves of any kind allowed). These Health Point losses are first allocated towards Rank-and-File models, and once enough Health Points losses are suffered to remove all Rank-and-File models, any remaining Health Point losses are allocated by the owner towards Attachable Models, as evenly as possible. Those Health Point losses can be reduced in the following ways: • If the unit contains Stubborn, the Health Point losses are halved, rounding fractions up. • If the unit is affected by Beacon of Courage, the Health Point losses are reduced by 1. • If the unit is Steady while affected by Beacon of Courage, the Health Point losses are reduced by an additional 1. • If the unit is Solid while affected by Beacon of Courage, the Health Point losses are reduced by an additional 1. I.e. a unit that is affected by Beacon of Courage while also being Steadfast reduces its Health Point losses by a total of 3. Attachable Models with Unstable can only join units containing Unstable, and units containing Unstable can only be joined by Attachable Models with Unstable.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Weapon Enchantments are upgrades that enhance weapons. A weapon on which a Weapon Enchantment is applied becomes an Enchanted Weapon. The Army List must indicate which weapon that the model is equipped with is an Enchanted Weapon (reminder: models are equipped with a Hand Weapon by default). Each Weapon Enchantment can only enchant particular weapon types (e.g. Great Weapon) or a category of weapons (e.g. Melee Weapon). The following rules apply to all Enchanted Weapons, unless specifically mentioned otherwise: • If a model is equipped with an Enchanted Weapon it must use it in Combat whenever possible. • All attacks made with the Enchanted Weapon gain Magical Attacks. • The Enchanted Weapon follows the rules for both its original weapon type and the Weapon Enchantment. • See the rules for weapons (Model Rules) for details on when to apply modifiers and additional rules.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Weapons is a subcategory of Model Rules. Just as with Attack Attributes, a Weapon can only be used by the specific model part with the rule. There are two types of weapons: • Melee Weapon: a model part can only use a single Melee Weapon at a time, and only when Engaged in Combat. If a model part is equipped with multiple Melee Weapons, the weapon it uses is determined in the First Round of Combat, with the following priority order: • An Enchanted Weapon • Any weapon that is neither a Hand Weapon, nor an Innate Weapon • A Hand Weapon • An Innate Weapon This choice is then kept until the model is no longer Engaged in Combat. The effects of Melee Weapons only apply to the model part’s Standard Melee Attacks. • If the Melee Weapon confers any modifier to Offensive Characteristics, as well as Attack Attributes, those effects are applied only to the model part’s Standard Melee Attacks. • If the Melee Weapon confers any modifier to Global or Defensive Characteristics (Charge Speed, Mobility, Courage, Defensive Skill, Hit Points, Resilience, and Armour), as well as Model Rules that are not Attack Attributes, those effects are applied to the whole model (or model part, see rules for Character Mounts for details when and how the Characteristics of mounts are affected) at all times, except while using a different Melee Weapon. • If the Melee Weapon confers any variable modifier (such as those based on a dice roll), the value of that modifier is determined at the start of the Agility Step in which the weapon is used. • Shooting Weapons: Shooting Weapons are used for making Shooting Attacks. Each model part can only use one Shooting Weapon per phase. A Shooting Weapon generally has an Aim value, shown in brackets after the name of the weapon. The rules for each Shooting Weapon define its maximum Range, the number of Shots fired per attack, its attacks’ Strength and Armour Penetration, as well as any potential Attack Attributes applied to them.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: During the Melee Phase, models that are in contact with an enemy Unit Boundary when their designated Agility Step is reached must attack. Except if they have been removed as a casualty. Restricted Attacks The rules for Restricted Attacks are used for Standard Melee Attacks in two circumstances: • Supporting Attacks: models in the second rank can use Standard Melee Attacks against enemies across models in the first rank, directly in front of them (i.e. only against models Engaged with the Front Facing of their unit). • Flank and Rear: Restricted Attacks apply when a model allocates Standard Melee Attacks towards an enemy that is Engaged with its Flank or Rear Facing. When a model intends to allocate any of its Standard Melee Attacks as Restricted Attacks, the total Standard Melee Attacks its combined model parts can make is never greater than its Height. If the model has multiple model parts (see Models and Units in the Definitions and Terminology chapter), its owner may decide which attacks from what model parts are used, as long as the total number of attacks for the combined model does not exceed its Height. For example, a Height 2 model consisting of a Knight (Att 2) on a Horse (Att 1) is making Supporting Attacks. This model can only perform 2 Standard Melee Attacks, and choose to first perform 1 attack with the Knight, and then at a lower Agility Step, 1 attack with the Horse. Fighting Over Gaps Models are considered to be in contact with each other across gaps. This can happen if there are gaps in a unit formation, or if units are not perfectly aligned with each other. To check if they are in contact, extend their bases in the direction of the Facing the unit is Engaged in. If this contacts an enemy model on the Facing it is Engaged with, both models are considered to be in contact with each other. The base cannot be extended past Impassable Terrain or a Unit Boundary belonging to a different unit. See images below for examples. Fighting over Gaps. – Left panel: Gaps in the unit formation. Models from the blue and red units are considered to be in contact over the gap indicated by the arrows a, b, and c. – Right panel: Imperfectly aligned units. The units are not perfectly aligned, but blue and red units are still considered to be in contact over the gap indicated by the arrows d and e.

characteristics.name: Rule
characteristics.$text: Normally, only models in the first and second rank can shoot. If different models in the unit have different types of Shooting Attacks, declare which one is used for each model. Each model can use their own Shooting Attacks. Determine which models in the Shooting unit can shoot: • The model must be able to draw Line of Sight to at least one model in the Target unit. • The model must have the target Health Pool within the Range of its Shooting Attack: measure this from each model in the unit to the closest point of the Target unit’s Boundary. Models that are outside their weapon’s Range cannot shoot. • All models in the Shooting unit must shoot at the same Target unit, but may, when possible, allocate their attacks towards different Health Pools within the targeted unit (see Allocating Attacks for rules on when Attachable Models joined to units may be chosen as the target). • Any model part in the unit can choose not to shoot.

Within the brackets of the rule, X will be given as a number and Y as one or more Paths, separated by commas. When the model is recruited, or gains this Universal Rule, the controlling player must choose one of those Paths. The Wizard will use that Path for the remainder of the campaign and must immediately generate X spells from it (see The 9th Age: Skirmish Campaigns – Paths for details). characteristics.$text: During Choosing Equipment and Abilities, the Black Rose must select one of the following Dances, with Duration: Round of Combat. The Black Rose cannot select a specific Dance again until one or more of the following has occurred: • She is not Engaged in Combat. • She has selected all Dances. • She can only select Dance of Caedhren, and it is not possible to do the Make Way. Dances: • Dance of Caedhren: the Black Rose can use Make Way, even if she is already in contact with an enemy model, provided she moves into contact with an enemy Character in her unit’s Front Facing. • Dance of Ceinran: Nominate one enemy Character model in contact with the Black Rose.
